She gives the stick a long, hard look, replaces it, then returns to the chest of drawers. Opening another one, the kitsune takes out a slip of paper and hands it to you. "Read it," she says. "For your eyes only." All right. You take the little slip from Kiyoko's fingers, unfurl it, and see what the future holds for you... [rand|You will soon receive a lucky windfall. It need not be great; it may be indeed but a small boon, but it will come at a most convenient time. Remember to give thanks to the Seven when you receive your boon. |Something unexpected lurks about you, shadowing your every step. Hope to be pleasantly surprised — but also be on your guard. |Avoid large bodies of water for a little while if you can. No good will come out of them for either you or those you care about. If you must venture near one, turn your back to it and toss a rock over your shoulder into the depths. It won't dispel your bad luck, but will mitigate the worst of it. |A circle of stones, a ring of mushrooms, a grove of trees. A range of mountains, a season of storms, a hail of arrows. |A foe prepares for your arrival. Prepare to meet them with equal force. Haste is of the essence; the longer you tarry, the more time they have to ready themselves. Strike a balance between gathering your strength and pushing on into the fray. |Misfortune lies in your future, though not immediate. There is not much you can do about it; struggle will only make your pain worse. Brace yourself as best as you can, and leave this warning out of your mind. |The next few days may hold an important choice that there will be no turning back from. Do not rush your decision, but take your time and choose wisely. The effects may not be immediately apparent, but they will most definitely make themselves felt in time. ] When you're done, you fold up the paper once more and hand it back to Kiyoko. What now? "Usually, you'd be expected to take good fortunes with you, and pin bad ones to a tree in the hopes of leaving them behind." Kiyoko gives you a small, sad smile. "But since you can't do that here, I'll just take it back, if you don't mind." "Now then... can we please move on?"'

rows.original: For better or for worse, you want to know.
rows.translation: 无论结果是好是坏，你都想知道。
rows.raw: "For better or for worse, you want to know."

rows.original: On second thought, maybe you'll pass on gazing too deeply into the waters of the future. "Thank you." Kiyoko heaves a small sigh of relief. "Trust me, I've read my own fortune enough times to know; topmost on my mind was always 'will I ever get out of here?'. The answers were vague at best, disheartening at worst... since then, I've given up trying to find out. It's better that way." Yeah, you understand. She's not refusing to spite you or anything. Kiyoko wiggles her large fox ears. "[pc.name], do you think I'm capable of spite?" Haha, all right. You get the point. Time to turn the conversation in another direction, then.
rows.translation: 仔细想想，或许你最好不要过度深入地探索未来的奥秘。 谢谢。 清子轻轻松了一口气。 相信我，我自己算过太多次命了，所以很清楚：我最关心的总是“我到底能不能离开这里？”而得到的答案，往好了说也是模棱两可，往坏了说就是令人沮丧的……从那以后，我就不再试图去寻找答案了。这样反而更好。 是的，你明白的。她并不是故意要惹你生气或做什么别的。 清子晃了晃她那对大大的狐狸耳朵。 "[pc.name]你以为我会有心怀怨恨的能力吗？ 哈哈，好吧，你明白我的意思了。那我们就把话题转向别的方向吧。
rows.raw: " On second thought, maybe you'll pass on gazing too deeply into the waters of the future. "Thank you." Kiyoko heaves a small sigh of relief. "Trust me, I've read my own fortune enough times to know; topmost on my mind was always 'will I ever get out of here?'. The answers were vague at best, disheartening at worst... since then, I've given up trying to find out. It's better that way." Yeah, you understand. She's not refusing to spite you or anything. Kiyoko wiggles her large fox ears. "[pc.name], do you think I'm capable of spite?" Haha, all right. You get the point. Time to turn the conversation in another direction, then."

rows.original: Ask Kiyoko to divine your future for you.
rows.translation: 让纪代子为你占卜未来吧。
rows.raw: "Ask Kiyoko to divine your future for you."

rows.original: You've already asked Kiyoko to divine your fortune for today. Don't push fate — it might just push back.
rows.translation: 你已经让清子为你预测今天的运势了。不要强行干预命运，否则它可能会反过来惩罚你。
rows.raw: "You've already asked Kiyoko to divine your fortune for today. Don't push fate — it might just push back."

rows.original: So, can she tell you something of her patron deity? "It wouldn't be right of me to speak of him behind his back," Kiyoko replies, her ears twitching and swivelling this way and that, as if expecting the deity himself to step out of thin air. "However, there are very many well-known fables about his exploits, and learning about what he's reputedly done might give you some insight into my master. Would you like to hear one of them?" Well, since you asked the question, there can't be any harm in it, can there? Kiyoko nods, moistens her throat with a sip of tea, and begins.
rows.translation: 那么，她能跟你讲讲她所信仰的主神吗？ 我背着他谈论他，这样做是不妥的。 清子回答道，她的耳朵不停地抽动着，来回转动着，仿佛期待着那位神明真的会从空气中出现一样。 然而，关于他的种种事迹，有许多广为流传的寓言故事。了解那些关于他的传说，或许能帮助你更好地理解我的主人。你想听其中一个故事吗？ 嗯，既然你提出了这个问题，那么问出来也没什么坏处吧？ 清子点了点头，喝了一口茶润了润喉咙，然后开始讲述起来。
rows.raw: ' So, can she tell you something of her patron deity? "It wouldn't be right of me to speak of him behind his back," Kiyoko replies, her ears twitching and swivelling this way and that, as if expecting the deity himself to step out of thin air. "However, there are very many well-known fables about his exploits, and learning about what he's reputedly done might give you some insight into my master. Would you like to hear one of them?" Well, since you asked the question, there can't be any harm in it, can there? Kiyoko nods, moistens her throat with a sip of tea, and begins.'

rows.original: [rand|The Sultan, ruler of Jassira, was proud and thought himself the cleverest man in the realm. It was true that he was extremely learned, and a man such as he enjoyed calling scholars from all over Savarra to ask them questions none could answer. What fun it was to flaunt his wit and shame others as he did! "Where is the center of the world?" the Sultan would ask, and then laugh when none could reply. Of course, he himself did not know the answer, but by his asking of the question, everyone assumed that he knew it — or was too cowed by his station to suggest otherwise. So happy was he with his scheme that he issued a proclamation: "The one who can tell me where the center of the world is shall receive all the wealth of Jassira. However, answer wrongly and you will receive only death." Who didn't want a fortune? Yet few were willing to risk execution to meet the Sultan's challenge — up until the day a strange, spindly catfolk dressed in motley yellow came up to the Sultan's palace. "I wish to meet the Sultan's challenge," he said. This was something which none had dared before, and soon the entire court had gathered while the catfolk was brought in his rags before the Sultan. "So, you wish to answer my riddle? Know that if your answer is wrong, then death awaits you." "I know this." "Very well. Where is the center of the world?" The stranger gave a sly grin before the Sultan's court, making sure all the noble lords and ladies of the catfolk had their eyes on him. "Why, right under my feet. It goes wherever I go, oh Sultan; as I move, so does the center of the world." "That's insane!" the Sultan exclaimed. "Is it? Well, oh great Sultan, if I'm wrong, bring us the world and we shall measure it together. Surely a lowly commoner like me can be easily proven wrong." The Sultan sputtered, the Sultan grumbled. Here was someone who had called his bluff! Yet he was not about to give a fortune to a mere man in rags! "That riddle was just the first. Here is another one: how many stars are in the sky?" "Neither too many nor too few," the stranger answered calmly. "That's not an answer!" the Sultan roared. "It's not? Then we shall go up together to the heavens and count the stars, oh Sultan. Then and only then may I be proven wrong." "Ridiculous," the sultan snarled. "Impossible. Very well, vagabond, I lay before you a final question: how many hairs are there on my head?" "As many as there are on my tail," came the reply. "Wrong!" the Sultan cried, leaping up from his jewelled throne and making as if to strangle the stranger where he stood. "That is wrong!" "Ah, but before you can be sure of that, oh wise Sultan, you must first count the hairs on both your hair and on my tail." The Sultan had enough of being made a fool of by this no-name stranger, doubly so in front of his court. With the whispers running through the lords and ladies of the catfolk, he knew that the story would spread — and there was nothing he could do to contain it. But at least he could make an example of this stranger who had dared to shame him this way. "Guards!" the Sultan cried. "Seize this cretin!" Before anyone could lay a hand on the stranger, though, the rags fell away from his body, and the catfolk was now a very vulpine and handsome man. As gasps ran through the court and many sought to prostrate themselves before Keros, the Trickster stepped up to the Sultan and gave the lord of the catfolk a mocking bow. "You think yourself clever, oh Sultan, and indeed you are so. But always remember that there are always those more clever than you." With a laugh, the Trickster vanished from sight, but that was not the last of it. When the Sultan later checked on his treasury, it had been utterly and completely emptied of all the wealth of Jassira. |Keros was minding his own peaceful business one day, walking through the streets of the capital in his favorite guise of an amber-furred catfolk in rags. Suddenly he saw two young men coming his way, and it was clear from their face they were in trouble. "What's wrong?" the Trickster asked, going up to them. "Can I help you?" The young men exchanged worried sighs. One of them looked at his companion, who nodded. "We are in terrible trouble. You see, ten months ago we came to the capital to find work. We were tired and hungry, so much so that we could not go any further, and so we stopped in a restaurant. There we ordered two eggs for each of us, a total of four boiled and pickled ones — but after we had eaten, we discovered we had no money left! To our eternal shame, we were forced to sneak out without paying." The Trickster frowned. "Is that it? Then go back and pay what you owe!" "That's what we did!" the second man exclaimed. "We finally managed to find work, and just the other day we returned to the restaurant and tried to pay the owner the single copper piece we owed him for the eggs. We told him our story, confessed our shame, and wished to make amends." "That sounds like a fair price for four eggs," Keros agreed. "That's the problem! The owner would not take it!" "Oh? Was he rewarding you for your honesty?" "Just the opposite! He claimed that if we'd not eaten the eggs, they'd have become chickens. Those chickens would have laid more eggs, and in these ten months he'd have perhaps thirty or so chickens from those selfsame eggs. He wants us to pay the full price — a whole fifty silvers — for these chickens he imagines he would have!" Keros' frown deepened. "There is more to this story, is there not?" "Well, the restaurant owner has now gone to the magistrate and lodged a complaint against us. The trial is in two days — and we can't pay that much! We'll be thrown in prison!" "This will not happen," Keros told the young men. "Go to the courthouse, and register my name — Tau — as a witness. Say that I may be found at this address." And he gave it to them. "But you weren't there!" the men protested. "Little matter, do it anyway. If you're going to prison, what do you have to lose?" Swayed by the Trickster's reasoning, the two young men agreed. When the day of the trial dawned, they went before the magistrate and asked him to enter the name Keros had given as a witness. The magistrate was annoyed, but such a thing was within the bounds of Belharan law, and so he had to agree. The magistrate called once, his voice ringing about the courtroom, but there was no ragged catfolk. He called again, with little effect. Turning to his bailiff, the magistrate said, "It seems like this witness isn't here. Go to this address and bring this Tau to me. I've half a mind to charge him for contempt of court." The bailiff took a number of soldiers and arrived at the address, a small shack by the slums. "By order of the Emperor's Law, Tau, you are to come with us." "Go away!" Keros replied from within the shack. "I'm very, very busy!" The bailiff wasn't about to leave empty handed. Kicking down the door, he ordered his soldiers to seize Keros, and seize him they did, dragging the rag-clad catfolk by the arms out into the streets and to the courthouse. Keros complained each step of the way that he was busy, oh so busy! At last, they made it back before the magistrate and hurled Keros to the ground. "Why are you so late?" the magistrate demanded. Keros waved his hands in the air. "I told your soldiers, I was too busy!" "And what task is so important that you can't come to a court of law?" "Oh, honorable magistrate, tomorrow I must begin my planting. I am going to grow wheat, and as such I have to boil enough wheat to sow all my fields. It's a long and laborious process, and as such I've been busy since before dawn." "Preposterous! How can one expect boiled wheat to sprout!" "Then how," Keros said sternly, looking straight at the restaurant owner, "can one expect boiled eggs to hatch into chickens?" The case was thrown out. |Once, Keros was at archery practice with three of his students. The Trickster set up a straw target in the shape of a bird, setting it in the high branches of a tree. The first student came up to him, bowed, and said: "Master, I am ready to begin." "Very good," Keros replied. "Do you see the bird?" "I do, Master." "And do you see the branch?" "I do, Master." "And the leaves?" "I do, Master." So on it went, with the rest of the tree, then the hills, then the sky. At the end of this questioning, Keros simply shook his head and bade the first student return to the bench. Now it was time for the second student's turn, and he, too, answered the questions the same way. Once again, Keros shook his head and bade the student sit back down. Now it was the third and final student's turn. "Do you see the bird?" Keros asked. "No, Master. All I see is the bird's eye." Keros smiled. "Draw your bow. We shall see what you've learned." The third student loosed an arrow at the straw bird, and hit it right in the eye. |A man dies — one of those mundane yet unfortunate deaths, like a mine cave-in or an accident with the plow — and finds himself in a dense forest aflower with fine cherry blossoms. Sunlight filters down through the canopy, but there are no shadows; the trees are thick enough to be impassable, but floating blue flames hanging in the air mark out a path. Seeing little choice, the man follows the dancing flames and happens upon a glade in the forest. From the other side of the clearing, he sees someone approaching. It is the trickster god Keros, immediately apparent by his vulpine nature, nine tails, and the bow slung over his shoulder. As the Trickster comes closer, it becomes apparent he is heading for a chair and table which had not been noticed before, but seem to have always been there, as objects are in dreams. The deity sits and takes out a large scroll from under the table, unfurling it and poring over its contents. "Ah, yes, you have lived a middling life, I see. Not good, not bad, but more on the side of good with a heavy dose of self-centeredness than anything else," he says. "That is about average; to be honest, I'm not sure why you're falling under my jurisdiction, but things are what they are. You were of reasonable intelligence, so you and your ancestors did something right in previous incarnations. This means I can offer you a choice." The Trickster claps his hands, and two shoji screen doors appear in the air. Rolling up the scroll, Keros steps between the two of them, and gives the man a deep, respectful bow. "Allow us to begin with the first door. Behind this door lies an easy existence; your job will be to raise butterflies. You will have a large greenhouse, and each day you must collect leaves with eggs on them before placing them in incubation trays. Then, when they hatch into caterpillars, you must feed them leaves that you grow. When each caterpillar forms a chrysalis, you must relocate it to the hatching chamber and wait for the metamorphosis to be complete, then release the butterfly after its wings dry." "You will live in a grand, luxurious mansion. Your job will take about three hours a day. You will dine at a fine restaurant for two meals, plus takeaway for lunch. But, the butterflies you release will fly upward out of the greenhouse and into infinite empty space where they will be destroyed. You will watch the results of your labor vanish into meaningless nothingness before your eyes, every day." "Now, for the second door. You will live in a small stone hut on a medium-sized island with rocky soil. Here, you will labor in clearing the land and planting it with the only crop that grows on this island, cabbage. You will survive on cabbage and the meat of an occasional goat, if you can bring down one of the wild ones that range the island. It is a hard and grueling life." "On this island are deer who love cabbage. They will not take it of their own accord, but whatever you bring to them, they will eat. You will not be allowed to eat them, either. But you will be able to observe them and the effects of your care upon them." The man becomes aware of a sensation that through its contrast to what he had been experiencing, reveals the shift in sensations that has occurred after death. He has not felt alive, but upon this decision, he feels more like he did when he was alive: a kind of trepidation mixed with hope, a sensitivity like cold air across his skin coupled with the loveliest, most carefree night. And yet, this choice is hard. The answer is obvious, and at the same time, it is not. He likes fine restaurants and large houses. The void, however, that is the thing. He thinks hard and gets nowhere. As he gives up on the decision and on himself for being too useless to make the choice, a memory comes back to him. His first daughter, with her first doll, which some years later had become ripped. He had taken it and re-stuffed it carefully, then mended the rents with rough twine he kept in the storehouse out back. Then he gave it back to her, not having told her what he was going to do, and observed to his surprise a look of ineffable joy on her face. Keros is watching him. "I see that your decision is made," he says, giving the man another bow. "So it must be. Good luck, and perhaps I will see you again soon." |One warm spring morning, Keros is napping at his shrine, having transformed into a bestial fox and curled up into a tight little ball. However, his nap is interrupted by a loud crashing coming from the forest path, two sets of quick footfalls, and he perks his head up sleepily as two women come running up the forest path, headed directly for his shrine. Barely has he woken up before the first woman throws herself before the Trickster, dragging the second in tow behind her. "Oh Lord Keros, I am in dire need of your judgement on a matter of law!" Sleepy and grouchy, the Trickster eyes the two women. "Do I look like a magistrate to you? Get yourselves to a courthouse." "Oh no, Lord Keros. As a Living God, your wisdom is great, and surely your judgement will be truer than any mere mortal magistrate. Furthermore, the local magistrate has been summoned to the Emperor's court and will not be here for the better part of this month." Keros sighs at the attempt at flattery, resigns himself to the fact that his nap is ruined, and sits up on his haunches. "Fine, fine. What is your dispute? This should be obvious, but I suggest you do not attempt to deceive a living god, especially one such as me." The first woman is quick to reply. "Lord Keros, I accuse my neighbor of being a thief! I sell grilled fish from my home, and every morning I work hard to prepare my husband's catch for sale at market; a simple seasoning of oil and herbs over a charcoal grill. Imagine my shock when I found my neighbor stealing from it what was rightfully mine!" Keros glances at the second woman, still cowering a little from being in the god's presence and more than a little pale. "You haven't said anything yet, woman. Are you not going to defend yourself?" The second woman bows her head and speaks. "Lord Keros, it is true that my neighbor sells grilled fish for a living, and she prepares the grill every morning. My husband and I are poor folk, and cannot afford her wares, but while she grills the fish the most divine of aromas lingers in the air. We leave the window open, such that we may savour the scent of grilled fish while we have our simple breakfast. That's all." "And I clearly overheard her say that being able to enjoy the scent of grilled fish — which should be rightfully mine — was almost as good as eating it! Lord Keros, she is a thief!" Keros squeezes his eyes shut. He is not having a good day. The living god looks between the two women for a few seconds, then his gaze alights on the latter. "Do you have any money on you, woman?" "My Lord, my husband and I are poor —" "Two coins are all I require. Your neighbor is right — the scent of her grilled fish is rightfully hers, and she needs to be recompensed for her losses." The second woman bows her head, but dares not argue with the deity's judgement. She walks up and places two copper coins before Keros, who takes one in each of his forepaws and brings them together; the clink of metal against metal reverberates about the forest shrine. Once. Twice. Thrice. And then, the Trickster nods to the second woman. "Come. Take back your coins." The first woman looks bewildered. "But weren't you going to pay me, Lord Keros?" Keros swivels his stern gaze towards the first woman. "The appropriate price for the aroma of fish is the sound of money; you have been duly recompensed. Now, I suggest that you drop the matter, for am I not wise, and my judgement greater than that of any mere mortal?" ]
rows.translation: [rand|贾西拉的统治者苏丹自诩为这片土地上最聪明的人，他对此感到无比自豪。事实上，他的学识确实渊博，他常常邀请来自萨瓦拉各地的学者来回答那些连其他人都无法解答的问题。这样的举动，无疑让他能够尽情展示自己的智慧，同时让他人感到羞愧——这真是件无比有趣的事情啊！ 世界的中心在哪里？ 苏丹会提出这个问题，然后当没有人能够回答时，他会哈哈大笑。当然，他自己其实也不知道答案，但因为他提出了这个问题，所有人都以为他知道答案——或者是因为他的地位太高，没有人敢提出不同的意见。他对自己的这个计谋感到非常满意，于是颁布了一项公告： 谁能告诉我世界的中心在哪里，就能得到贾西拉所有的财富。但如果你答错了，等待你的只有死亡。 谁不想要一笔财富呢？然而，却很少有人愿意冒着被处死的危险去接受苏丹的挑战——直到有一天，一只穿着杂色黄衣服、身材瘦高的猫人来到了苏丹的宫殿。 我愿意接受苏丹的挑战。 他说。 这是前所未有的举动，不久整个宫廷的人都聚集了过来，而那个穿着破烂的猫人也被带到了苏丹面前。 那么，你愿意回答我的谜题吗？要知道，如果你的答案是错误的，死亡将会降临到你头上。 这个我懂。 很好。那么，世界的中心在哪里呢？ 那个陌生人在苏丹的宫廷前露出了狡黠的笑容，确保所有猫人的贵族们都能注意到他。 就在我的脚下啊。无论我走到哪里，它都会跟着我；我移动，世界的中心也随之移动。 太疯狂了！ 苏丹惊呼道。 是吗？那么，哦，伟大的苏丹，如果我错了，您就把整个世界拿给我们来看，让我们一起验证吧。像我这样的卑微平民，肯定很容易就被证明是错的。 苏丹嘟囔着，抱怨着。竟然有人看穿了他的把戏！但他绝对不会把一大笔财富送给一个衣衫褴褛的普通人！ 那个谜语只是第一个。这里还有一个：天空中有多少颗星星？ 不多也不少。 那个陌生人平静地回答道。 那根本不是个答案！ 苏丹怒吼起来。 不是吗？那么我们就一起登上天空，数数那些星星吧，哦，苏丹。只有到那时，我才能证明自己是错的。 太荒谬了。 苏丹怒吼道。 不可能。好吧，流浪者，我最后问你一个问题：我的头上一共有多少根头发？ 就像跟在我后面的那些人一样多。 回复来了。 错了！ 苏丹惊呼着从他那镶嵌着宝石的宝座上跳了起来，似乎想要当场掐死那个陌生人。 那不对！ 啊，但在你能够确定这一点之前，哦，睿智的苏丹，你首先必须数一数你自己头发上的头发数，以及我尾巴上的毛发数。 苏丹受够了被这个无名之辈愚弄，尤其是在他的宫廷面前。当这些谣言在猫人贵族们中传开时，他知道这件事一定会扩散开来——而他对此无能为力。 不过，至少他可以让这个敢于如此羞辱他的陌生人受到应有的惩罚。 卫兵！ 苏丹哭了。 抓住这个白痴！ 然而，在任何人来得及触碰那个陌生人之前，他身上的破布突然脱落了，那个猫人立刻变成了一个英俊潇洒的男子。当周围的人们发出惊呼声，许多人纷纷想要向凯罗斯跪拜时，那个骗子却走上前，对着这位猫人的统治者做了一个嘲讽的鞠躬。 你自以为很聪明，哦苏丹，的确如此。但请永远记住，总有人比你更聪明。 随着一声笑声，那个狡猾的家伙从人们的视线中消失了，但事情并没有就此结束。后来，当苏丹检查他的国库时，发现贾西拉的所有财富都已经被洗劫一空，国库里空空如也。 |有一天，凯罗斯正安安静静地做着自己的事，他以自己最喜欢的装扮——一只穿着破旧衣服、毛色呈琥珀色的猫人——在首都的街道上漫步。突然，他看到有两个年轻人朝他的方向走来，从他们的表情来看，他们显然遇到了麻烦。 怎么了？ 那个骗子走上前，问道。 需要帮忙吗？ 那些年轻人互相交换着担忧的目光。其中一个人看了看他的同伴，后者点了点头。 我们陷入了极大的麻烦。十个月前，我们来到首都寻找工作。那时我们又累又饿，实在走不动了，于是就在一家餐馆停了下来。我们在那里每人点了两个鸡蛋，总共四个，都是煮熟后腌制的——但吃完之后，我们才发现自己已经身无分文了！让我们永远蒙羞的是，我们不得不不付钱就偷偷溜走了。 那个捣蛋鬼皱起了眉头。 就这样吗？那你就回去把欠的钱还上吧！ 正是我们这么做的！ 第二个人惊叫道。 我们终于找到了工作，前几天我们回到了那家餐馆，想要把欠老板的那一枚铜币还给他——那是我们买鸡蛋时欠下的钱。我们向他讲述了我们的经历，表达了我们的歉意，也希望能弥补这个过错。 对于四个鸡蛋来说，这个价格似乎挺合理的。 凯罗斯同意了。 问题就在这里！老板根本不愿意接受它！ 哦？他是为了奖励你的诚实而这么做吗？ 恰恰相反！他声称，如果我们没有吃掉那些鸡蛋，它们就会变成小鸡。而这些小鸡会再下更多的蛋，这样一来，在这十个月里，他从那些鸡蛋里就能得到大约三十只小鸡。他现在要求我们为这些他想象中会存在的小鸡支付全额费用——整整五十枚银币！ 凯罗斯的眉头皱得更深了。 这件事背后肯定还有别的原因，对吧？ 嗯，餐厅老板现在已经去告发了我们，法官将在两天后开庭审理这个案子——而我们根本无力支付那么多的赔偿金！我们肯定会被关进监狱的！ 这种事是不会发生的。 凯罗斯对那些年轻人说道。 去法院，把我的名字——陶——登记为证人。说明我可以在这个地址找到。 然后他把它交给了他们。 但当时你并不在场啊！ 那些人提出了抗议。 没什么大不了的，反正都要去做。如果因此进监狱，你又能失去什么呢？ 在那个狡猾之人的说服下，这两名年轻人同意了。当审判的日子到来时，他们来到法官面前，请求法官将凯洛斯作为证人列入名单。法官感到有些恼火，但这种请求确实符合贝尔哈兰的法律，因此他不得不同意。 法官大声呼唤了一次，他的声音在法庭上回荡，但却没有出现那个衣衫褴褛的猫人。他又叫了一次，仍然没有效果。于是，法官转向他的法警，说道 看来这个证人不在这里。去这个地址把那个叫Tau的人带过来。我真想以藐视法庭的罪名起诉他。 法警带着几名士兵来到了那个地址——贫民区旁的一间小棚屋。 根据皇帝法令的命令，陶，你必须跟我们一起来。 走开！ 凯罗斯从小屋里回应道。 我真的很忙！ 法警绝对不会空手而归。他一脚踹开大门，命令士兵们抓住凯罗斯，士兵们果然照做了，他们抓住这个衣衫褴褛的猫人，将他拖到了街上，然后带到了法庭。凯罗斯一路上都在抱怨自己非常非常忙！ 终于，他们在法官面前将凯罗斯推到了地上。 你怎么会迟到呢？ 法官要求如此。 凯罗斯在空气中挥了挥手。 我告诉过你们的士兵，我当时太忙了！ 那么，有什么任务是如此重要，以至于你无法出庭受审呢？ 哦，尊敬的法官，明天我必须开始播种了。我打算种植小麦，因此需要煮足够多的小麦种子来播种所有的田地。这个过程既漫长又费力，所以从天还没亮我就已经开始忙碌了。 荒谬！怎么可能指望煮熟的麦粒还能发芽呢！ 那么，该如何做呢？ 凯罗斯严肃地说道，目光直视着餐厅老板。 难道有人会指望煮熟的鸡蛋能孵化出小鸡来吗？ 这个案件被驳回了。 |有一次，凯罗斯和他的三个学生一起进行射箭练习。那个爱搞恶作剧的家伙在树的高枝上挂了一个鸟形的稻草靶子。第一个学生走到他跟前，鞠了一躬，然后说道： 大师，我已经准备好了，可以开始了吗？ 非常好。 凯罗斯回答道。 你看到那只鸟了吗？ 是，主人。 那么，你看到那根树枝了吗？ 遵命，主人。 那那些叶子呢？ 遵命，主人。 就这样，接着是树的其他部分，然后是山丘，最后是天空。在这段问答结束后，凯罗斯只是摇了摇头，然后让第一个学生回到座位上。现在轮到第二个学生了，他也用同样的方式回答了问题。凯罗斯再次摇了摇头，让那个学生坐回去。 现在，轮到第三个，也是最后一个学生了。 你看到那只鸟了吗？ 凯罗斯问道。 不，主人。我所看到的只是一片鸟瞰图而已。 凯罗斯笑了。 拉弓吧，让我们看看你学到了什么。 第三个学生向那只草编鸟射出了一支箭，正好射中了它的眼睛。 |有一个人死了——死于那种平凡却又不幸的死亡方式，比如矿井坍塌或是使用犁具时发生的意外——然后他发现自己置身于一片开满美丽樱花的茂密森林之中。阳光透过树冠洒下来，但却没有形成任何阴影；这些树木长得太过茂密，根本无法通行，但空气中漂浮的蓝色火焰却为人们指出了前进的道路。 迫于无奈，这个男人跟随那些跳跃的火焰，在森林中找到了一片空地。 从空地的另一边，他看到有人正在靠近。那是欺诈之神凯罗斯——他的狐狸般的外表、九条尾巴以及肩上悬挂的弓，立刻让人认出了他的身份。 当那个骗子逐渐靠近时，人们发现他正朝着一张椅子和一张桌子走去——这两件物品之前并未被注意到，但它们似乎一直就在那里，就像梦中的物品一样。那位神明坐下来，从桌子下面拿出一卷巨大的卷轴，展开它，开始仔细研读上面的文字。 啊，原来如此，你过着一种平平无奇的生活。不算好，也不算坏，但总体来说还是偏好的那一面，只不过其中自私的因素占了很大比重。 他说。 这还算平均水平吧。说实话，我不太明白为什么你会归我的管辖范围，但事实就是如此。你的智力还算不错，所以你在前世一定做了一些正确的事情，你的祖先们也是如此。因此，我可以给你一个选择。 戏法师拍手示意，两扇障子门便凭空出现。凯罗斯卷起卷轴，从这两扇门之间穿过，然后向那位男子深深地鞠了一躬，表示尊敬。 让我们先从第一扇门开始说起。这扇门后面是一份轻松的工作：你的任务就是饲养蝴蝶。你会拥有一个很大的温室，每天都需要采集那些带有虫卵的叶子，然后将它们放入孵化箱中。当幼虫孵化出来后，你需要用自己种植的叶子来喂养它们。当每只幼虫都结成蛹时，你就需要把它们转移到孵化室里，等待它们完成变态过程，等到翅膀干透后，再将蝴蝶放出来。 你将居住在一座宏伟豪华的宅邸中。你的工作每天只需要大约三个小时。你会有两顿饭在高档餐厅享用，午餐还会外带。然而，你释放的那些蝴蝶会飞出温室，进入无边无际的虚空，在那里它们将会消失殆尽。每天，你都将亲眼看到自己辛勤劳动的成果在眼前化为无意义的虚无。 现在，来看第二种选择。你将生活在一个土壤多石的中等大小的岛上，那里有一间小石屋。在这里，你需要辛勤劳作，开垦土地，并种植这种岛上唯一能生长的作物——卷心菜。你的食物将主要来自卷心菜，偶尔也能捕到一些野山羊，如果能够成功捕捉到它们的话。这样的生活十分艰辛且充满挑战。 在这个岛上，生活着一些喜欢吃卷心菜的鹿。它们不会主动去吃卷心菜，但无论你给它们带来什么食物，它们都会吃。不过，你也不被允许吃这些鹿。不过，你可以观察它们，以及你的照顾对它们产生的影响。 这个人开始注意到一种感觉，这种感觉与他之前所经历的一切形成了鲜明的对比，从而让他意识到死亡之后，自己的感官体验确实发生了变化。他之前从未真正感受到过“活着”的感觉，但在这个时刻，他突然觉得自己又恢复了生前的那种状态：一种既紧张又充满希望的情绪，一种如同冷空气掠过皮肤般的敏锐感觉，同时又伴随着最为美好、最为无忧无虑的夜晚氛围。 然而，这个选择实在很难做出。答案看似显而易见，却又似乎并非如此。他喜欢高档餐厅和宽敞的住宅，但问题恰恰就在于这一点——他苦思冥想，却始终找不到解决办法。 就在他开始放弃这个决定，也开始责怪自己太无能、无法做出选择的时候，一段回忆突然浮现在他的脑海中。 他的第一个女儿，和她的第一个玩偶——几年后，那个玩偶已经破旧不堪了。他把它拿过来，仔细地重新填充了填充物，然后用储存在后院仓库里的粗麻绳修补了那些破洞。然后他把玩偶还给了女儿，却没有告诉她自己做了这些事情。令他惊讶的是，他看到女儿脸上露出了难以形容的喜悦之情。 凯罗斯正在注视着他。 我看你已经做出了决定。 他说着，又向那个男人鞠了一躬。 果然如此。祝你好运，也许不久后我们还会再见面。 |一个温暖的春日早晨，凯罗斯变成了一只野狐狸，蜷缩在他的神龛旁小睡。然而，森林小路上突然传来的巨响和急促的脚步声打断了他的休息。他昏昏沉沉地抬起头，看到两个女人正沿着小路朝他的神龛方向奔来。还没等他完全清醒，第一个女人就已经扑到了那个“骗子”面前，还将第二个女人拽在了身后。 哦，凯罗斯大人，我在一件法律问题上迫切需要您的裁决！ 困倦又脾气暴躁的捣蛋鬼盯着那两个女人。 在我看来，我像法官吗？快去法院吧。 哦不，凯罗斯大人。作为一位活生生的神明，您的智慧无比高深，您的判断肯定比任何凡人的法官都要公正。更何况，当地的法官已经被召往皇帝的宫廷，这个月的大部分时间他都不会在这里。 凯罗斯对这种奉承话感到无奈，只好认命，觉得自己的小憩已经泡汤了，于是便坐了起来。 好吧好吧，你们到底有什么争执？这应该很明显才对，但我建议你们不要试图欺骗一位活生生的神明，尤其是像我这样的神明。 第一位女性很快就回复了。 凯罗斯大人，我指控我的邻居是个小偷！我在家里卖烤鱼，每天早上都会认真地将我丈夫捕来的鱼进行处理，然后拿到市场上售卖——只需要在炭火烤架上加入一些油和香草作为调味料而已。当我发现我的邻居偷走了本该属于我的东西时，我简直惊呆了！ 凯罗斯瞥了瞥第二位女性，她仍然因为身处这位神明面前而有些畏缩，脸色也显得相当苍白。 你到现在还没说一句话，女人。难道你就不打算为自己辩护吗？ 第二位女性低下头，开口说道。 凯罗斯大人，的确，我的邻居以售卖烤鱼为生，她每天早上都会准备烤架。我和我丈夫都是穷人，买不起她的食物，但每当她烤鱼的时候，空气中就会弥漫着那种极其美妙的香气。我们会把窗户打开，这样在吃简单的早餐时就能享受到烤鱼的香味。就是这么简单。 我清楚地听到她说过，能够闻到烤鱼的味道——那本来应该是我的享受——就已经让人感觉几乎像真正吃到了鱼一样美味了！凯罗斯大人，她简直就是个小偷！ 凯罗斯紧闭双眼，今天他实在过得很不顺心。这位“活神”在两位女性之间扫视了几秒钟，最终将目光停在了后一位身上。 女人，你身上带钱吗？ 大人，我和我的丈夫都很穷…… 我只需要两枚硬币而已。你的邻居说得对——她烤鱼的香味确实属于她，她应该得到相应的补偿来弥补自己的损失。 第二位女子低下了头，但她不敢质疑神的裁决。她走上前，在凯罗斯面前放了两枚铜币。凯罗斯用它的前爪各抓起一枚硬币，然后将它们碰在了一起；金属相互碰撞发出的声响在森林中的神殿里回荡。 一次。两次。三次。然后，那个狡猾的角色向第二位女子点了点头。 过来，把你的硬币拿回去吧。 第一位女性看起来显得十分困惑。 但是您不是说要付我钱的吗，凯罗斯大人？ 凯罗斯将目光转向了第一位女性。 对于鱼香而言，恰当的代价就是金钱；你已经得到了应有的回报。现在，我建议你放弃这件事吧，因为我不正是智慧的象征吗？我的判断力，难道还比不上任何一个凡人吗？ ]
rows.raw: ' [rand|The Sultan, ruler of Jassira, was proud and thought himself the cleverest man in the realm. It was true that he was extremely learned, and a man such as he enjoyed calling scholars from all over Savarra to ask them questions none could answer. What fun it was to flaunt his wit and shame others as he did! "Where is the center of the world?" the Sultan would ask, and then laugh when none could reply. Of course, he himself did not know the answer, but by his asking of the question, everyone assumed that he knew it — or was too cowed by his station to suggest otherwise. So happy was he with his scheme that he issued a proclamation: "The one who can tell me where the center of the world is shall receive all the wealth of Jassira. However, answer wrongly and you will receive only death." Who didn't want a fortune? Yet few were willing to risk execution to meet the Sultan's challenge — up until the day a strange, spindly catfolk dressed in motley yellow came up to the Sultan's palace. "I wish to meet the Sultan's challenge," he said. This was something which none had dared before, and soon the entire court had gathered while the catfolk was brought in his rags before the Sultan. "So, you wish to answer my riddle? Know that if your answer is wrong, then death awaits you." "I know this." "Very well. Where is the center of the world?" The stranger gave a sly grin before the Sultan's court, making sure all the noble lords and ladies of the catfolk had their eyes on him. "Why, right under my feet. It goes wherever I go, oh Sultan; as I move, so does the center of the world." "That's insane!" the Sultan exclaimed. "Is it? Well, oh great Sultan, if I'm wrong, bring us the world and we shall measure it together. Surely a lowly commoner like me can be easily proven wrong." The Sultan sputtered, the Sultan grumbled. Here was someone who had called his bluff! Yet he was not about to give a fortune to a mere man in rags! "That riddle was just the first. Here is another one: how many stars are in the sky?" "Neither too many nor too few," the stranger answered calmly. "That's not an answer!" the Sultan roared. "It's not? Then we shall go up together to the heavens and count the stars, oh Sultan. Then and only then may I be proven wrong." "Ridiculous," the sultan snarled. "Impossible. Very well, vagabond, I lay before you a final question: how many hairs are there on my head?" "As many as there are on my tail," came the reply. "Wrong!" the Sultan cried, leaping up from his jewelled throne and making as if to strangle the stranger where he stood. "That is wrong!" "Ah, but before you can be sure of that, oh wise Sultan, you must first count the hairs on both your hair and on my tail." The Sultan had enough of being made a fool of by this no-name stranger, doubly so in front of his court. With the whispers running through the lords and ladies of the catfolk, he knew that the story would spread — and there was nothing he could do to contain it. But at least he could make an example of this stranger who had dared to shame him this way. "Guards!" the Sultan cried. "Seize this cretin!" Before anyone could lay a hand on the stranger, though, the rags fell away from his body, and the catfolk was now a very vulpine and handsome man. As gasps ran through the court and many sought to prostrate themselves before Keros, the Trickster stepped up to the Sultan and gave the lord of the catfolk a mocking bow. "You think yourself clever, oh Sultan, and indeed you are so. But always remember that there are always those more clever than you." With a laugh, the Trickster vanished from sight, but that was not the last of it. When the Sultan later checked on his treasury, it had been utterly and completely emptied of all the wealth of Jassira. |Keros was minding his own peaceful business one day, walking through the streets of the capital in his favorite guise of an amber-furred catfolk in rags. Suddenly he saw two young men coming his way, and it was clear from their face they were in trouble. "What's wrong?" the Trickster asked, going up to them. "Can I help you?" The young men exchanged worried sighs. One of them looked at his companion, who nodded. "We are in terrible trouble. You see, ten months ago we came to the capital to find work. We were tired and hungry, so much so that we could not go any further, and so we stopped in a restaurant. There we ordered two eggs for each of us, a total of four boiled and pickled ones — but after we had eaten, we discovered we had no money left! To our eternal shame, we were forced to sneak out without paying." The Trickster frowned. "Is that it? Then go back and pay what you owe!" "That's what we did!" the second man exclaimed. "We finally managed to find work, and just the other day we returned to the restaurant and tried to pay the owner the single copper piece we owed him for the eggs. We told him our story, confessed our shame, and wished to make amends." "That sounds like a fair price for four eggs," Keros agreed. "That's the problem! The owner would not take it!" "Oh? Was he rewarding you for your honesty?" "Just the opposite! He claimed that if we'd not eaten the eggs, they'd have become chickens. Those chickens would have laid more eggs, and in these ten months he'd have perhaps thirty or so chickens from those selfsame eggs. He wants us to pay the full price — a whole fifty silvers — for these chickens he imagines he would have!" Keros' frown deepened. "There is more to this story, is there not?" "Well, the restaurant owner has now gone to the magistrate and lodged a complaint against us. The trial is in two days — and we can't pay that much! We'll be thrown in prison!" "This will not happen," Keros told the young men. "Go to the courthouse, and register my name — Tau — as a witness. Say that I may be found at this address." And he gave it to them. "But you weren't there!" the men protested. "Little matter, do it anyway. If you're going to prison, what do you have to lose?" Swayed by the Trickster's reasoning, the two young men agreed. When the day of the trial dawned, they went before the magistrate and asked him to enter the name Keros had given as a witness. The magistrate was annoyed, but such a thing was within the bounds of Belharan law, and so he had to agree. The magistrate called once, his voice ringing about the courtroom, but there was no ragged catfolk. He called again, with little effect. Turning to his bailiff, the magistrate said, "It seems like this witness isn't here. Go to this address and bring this Tau to me. I've half a mind to charge him for contempt of court." The bailiff took a number of soldiers and arrived at the address, a small shack by the slums. "By order of the Emperor's Law, Tau, you are to come with us." "Go away!" Keros replied from within the shack. "I'm very, very busy!" The bailiff wasn't about to leave empty handed. Kicking down the door, he ordered his soldiers to seize Keros, and seize him they did, dragging the rag-clad catfolk by the arms out into the streets and to the courthouse. Keros complained each step of the way that he was busy, oh so busy! At last, they made it back before the magistrate and hurled Keros to the ground. "Why are you so late?" the magistrate demanded. Keros waved his hands in the air. "I told your soldiers, I was too busy!" "And what task is so important that you can't come to a court of law?" "Oh, honorable magistrate, tomorrow I must begin my planting. I am going to grow wheat, and as such I have to boil enough wheat to sow all my fields. It's a long and laborious process, and as such I've been busy since before dawn." "Preposterous! How can one expect boiled wheat to sprout!" "Then how," Keros said sternly, looking straight at the restaurant owner, "can one expect boiled eggs to hatch into chickens?" The case was thrown out. |Once, Keros was at archery practice with three of his students. The Trickster set up a straw target in the shape of a bird, setting it in the high branches of a tree. The first student came up to him, bowed, and said: "Master, I am ready to begin." "Very good," Keros replied. "Do you see the bird?" "I do, Master." "And do you see the branch?" "I do, Master." "And the leaves?" "I do, Master." So on it went, with the rest of the tree, then the hills, then the sky. At the end of this questioning, Keros simply shook his head and bade the first student return to the bench. Now it was time for the second student's turn, and he, too, answered the questions the same way. Once again, Keros shook his head and bade the student sit back down. Now it was the third and final student's turn. "Do you see the bird?" Keros asked. "No, Master. All I see is the bird's eye." Keros smiled. "Draw your bow. We shall see what you've learned." The third student loosed an arrow at the straw bird, and hit it right in the eye. |A man dies — one of those mundane yet unfortunate deaths, like a mine cave-in or an accident with the plow — and finds himself in a dense forest aflower with fine cherry blossoms. Sunlight filters down through the canopy, but there are no shadows; the trees are thick enough to be impassable, but floating blue flames hanging in the air mark out a path. Seeing little choice, the man follows the dancing flames and happens upon a glade in the forest. From the other side of the clearing, he sees someone approaching. It is the trickster god Keros, immediately apparent by his vulpine nature, nine tails, and the bow slung over his shoulder. As the Trickster comes closer, it becomes apparent he is heading for a chair and table which had not been noticed before, but seem to have always been there, as objects are in dreams. The deity sits and takes out a large scroll from under the table, unfurling it and poring over its contents. "Ah, yes, you have lived a middling life, I see. Not good, not bad, but more on the side of good with a heavy dose of self-centeredness than anything else," he says. "That is about average; to be honest, I'm not sure why you're falling under my jurisdiction, but things are what they are. You were of reasonable intelligence, so you and your ancestors did something right in previous incarnations. This means I can offer you a choice." The Trickster claps his hands, and two shoji screen doors appear in the air. Rolling up the scroll, Keros steps between the two of them, and gives the man a deep, respectful bow. "Allow us to begin with the first door. Behind this door lies an easy existence; your job will be to raise butterflies. You will have a large greenhouse, and each day you must collect leaves with eggs on them before placing them in incubation trays. Then, when they hatch into caterpillars, you must feed them leaves that you grow. When each caterpillar forms a chrysalis, you must relocate it to the hatching chamber and wait for the metamorphosis to be complete, then release the butterfly after its wings dry." "You will live in a grand, luxurious mansion. Your job will take about three hours a day. You will dine at a fine restaurant for two meals, plus takeaway for lunch. But, the butterflies you release will fly upward out of the greenhouse and into infinite empty space where they will be destroyed. You will watch the results of your labor vanish into meaningless nothingness before your eyes, every day." "Now, for the second door. You will live in a small stone hut on a medium-sized island with rocky soil. Here, you will labor in clearing the land and planting it with the only crop that grows on this island, cabbage. You will survive on cabbage and the meat of an occasional goat, if you can bring down one of the wild ones that range the island. It is a hard and grueling life." "On this island are deer who love cabbage. They will not take it of their own accord, but whatever you bring to them, they will eat. You will not be allowed to eat them, either. But you will be able to observe them and the effects of your care upon them." The man becomes aware of a sensation that through its contrast to what he had been experiencing, reveals the shift in sensations that has occurred after death. He has not felt alive, but upon this decision, he feels more like he did when he was alive: a kind of trepidation mixed with hope, a sensitivity like cold air across his skin coupled with the loveliest, most carefree night. And yet, this choice is hard. The answer is obvious, and at the same time, it is not. He likes fine restaurants and large houses. The void, however, that is the thing. He thinks hard and gets nowhere. As he gives up on the decision and on himself for being too useless to make the choice, a memory comes back to him. His first daughter, with her first doll, which some years later had become ripped. He had taken it and re-stuffed it carefully, then mended the rents with rough twine he kept in the storehouse out back. Then he gave it back to her, not having told her what he was going to do, and observed to his surprise a look of ineffable joy on her face. Keros is watching him. "I see that your decision is made," he says, giving the man another bow. "So it must be. Good luck, and perhaps I will see you again soon." |One warm spring morning, Keros is napping at his shrine, having transformed into a bestial fox and curled up into a tight little ball. However, his nap is interrupted by a loud crashing coming from the forest path, two sets of quick footfalls, and he perks his head up sleepily as two women come running up the forest path, headed directly for his shrine. Barely has he woken up before the first woman throws herself before the Trickster, dragging the second in tow behind her. "Oh Lord Keros, I am in dire need of your judgement on a matter of law!" Sleepy and grouchy, the Trickster eyes the two women. "Do I look like a magistrate to you? Get yourselves to a courthouse." "Oh no, Lord Keros. As a Living God, your wisdom is great, and surely your judgement will be truer than any mere mortal magistrate. Furthermore, the local magistrate has been summoned to the Emperor's court and will not be here for the better part of this month." Keros sighs at the attempt at flattery, resigns himself to the fact that his nap is ruined, and sits up on his haunches. "Fine, fine. What is your dispute? This should be obvious, but I suggest you do not attempt to deceive a living god, especially one such as me." The first woman is quick to reply. "Lord Keros, I accuse my neighbor of being a thief! I sell grilled fish from my home, and every morning I work hard to prepare my husband's catch for sale at market; a simple seasoning of oil and herbs over a charcoal grill. Imagine my shock when I found my neighbor stealing from it what was rightfully mine!" Keros glances at the second woman, still cowering a little from being in the god's presence and more than a little pale. "You haven't said anything yet, woman. Are you not going to defend yourself?" The second woman bows her head and speaks. "Lord Keros, it is true that my neighbor sells grilled fish for a living, and she prepares the grill every morning. My husband and I are poor folk, and cannot afford her wares, but while she grills the fish the most divine of aromas lingers in the air. We leave the window open, such that we may savour the scent of grilled fish while we have our simple breakfast. That's all." "And I clearly overheard her say that being able to enjoy the scent of grilled fish — which should be rightfully mine — was almost as good as eating it! Lord Keros, she is a thief!" Keros squeezes his eyes shut. He is not having a good day. The living god looks between the two women for a few seconds, then his gaze alights on the latter. "Do you have any money on you, woman?" "My Lord, my husband and I are poor —" "Two coins are all I require. Your neighbor is right — the scent of her grilled fish is rightfully hers, and she needs to be recompensed for her losses." The second woman bows her head, but dares not argue with the deity's judgement. She walks up and places two copper coins before Keros, who takes one in each of his forepaws and brings them together; the clink of metal against metal reverberates about the forest shrine. Once. Twice. Thrice. And then, the Trickster nods to the second woman. "Come. Take back your coins." The first woman looks bewildered. "But weren't you going to pay me, Lord Keros?" Keros swivels his stern gaze towards the first woman. "The appropriate price for the aroma of fish is the sound of money; you have been duly recompensed. Now, I suggest that you drop the matter, for am I not wise, and my judgement greater than that of any mere mortal?" ]'

rows.original: [kiyoko.pregStage 1 2 3 4|[rand|"Wery well. Very well indeed." Kiyoko looks very pleased with herself. "Want to know a secret?" Oh? What would that be? rows.raw: " At the mention of Kinu's name, Kiyoko gives you a thin-lipped smile. "Oh, her. Some days I love my [kiyoko.numKits 3|eldest ]daughter... and some days she exasperates me to the point where I wish I could stuff her back into where she came from." Just wait till she gets older. There's something about mothers and daughters that sets them to odds even in the most harmonious of families, isn't there? A sigh. "Now that I'm in my mother's position, I can't help but wonder if I was as much of a screaming handful all those years ago. Sure, it doesn't seem that way from my perspective, but then again I can't rely on myself to be honest when assessing my own behavior..." Well, for all her intelligence, Kinu is a child, and a kitsune at that; she'll have certain impulses and proclivities. Wisdom is something that's only gained with time. Kiyoko doesn't answer that, but sips furiously at her tea. [rand|"I know it's tempting to want to spoil our daughter, especially since you can't be here in the Astral Plane all the time," the kitsune mother says at last. "But please don't give her too many gifts." Now, you didn't — "I'm not accusing you of anything, [pc.name]. But our daughter is a terror when she'd had too many sweet things at once — she's practically bouncing off the walls and running across the ceiling, and won't sit still to study or be brushed. In fact, she becomes absolutely useless for any of her daily chores until she's exhausted herself and had a nap first." Goodness. "And that's only when she's had a bit too much. If I don't rein her in, she'll get into the peach grove and eat herself sick. I've somewhat managed to discipline that out of her, but your gifts to her are still considered fair game." All right, you get her point. "I'm not saying that you can't give our daughter gifts, but please try to keep it in moderation. That's all I ask. I don't want to find her lying on the hillside holding her tummy in pain, and discover that she tried to eat two whole sweet melons in one go. A less intelligent child might actually learn something from the experience, but she's great at rationalizing away her mistakes. Being smart doesn't necessarily mean that you behave more sensibly — if anything, it means making excuses for yourself all the easier." |So, how is her education proceeding? "Our daughter wants to be a den mother like me," Kiyoko replies. "I really should be flattered, shouldn't I?" Well, with such a great example to follow... "Hmph. Now don't you start as well. But yes, that's the way I'm taking her education in. Traditionally, the title is handed from mother to eldest daughter, but I get the feeling that there's a lot of empty land to be settled once we get out of here — and hence she'll get to be one sooner than expected." What sorts of things are passed down from one den mother to the next, anyway? "Right now I'm trying to improve our daughter's temperament. After all, beauty fades and the mind dulls with age, but a warm personality and pleasant temperament last till your dying day." A rather impressive undertaking, and one that probably is going to take some time; it doesn't sound like the thing that can be done overnight, and you don't think Kinu's astronomical rate of learning will help in this case. How is she going about it, though? "Having her do housework." That's all? A thin smile. "You underestimate the amount of housework than can potentially crop up here, [pc.name]. That goes double when I don't get the Astral Plane to re-order itself when messes crop up. And trust me, kitsune children tend to make a lot of messes." Ah... "Add that to the fact the kitsune children are boisterous and tend to get into all sorts of trouble, and one quickly learns to cultivate a positive temperament in the face of adversity that would have others screaming in exasperation. She will need it as a den mother." Kiyoko sets down her tea and pops a candy into her mouth, chewing thoughtfully. "You didn't think I came out of the womb this calm and genial all the time, did you?" Well... to be honest, you can see that happening. At the very least, she didn't cry much as a baby, did she? Kiyoko rolls her eyes, but smiles. "It's true I was a calm kit, but natural inclinations must still be carefully cultivated to reach their zenith. I'm doing that with our daughter — just relax and leave her education to me." |"Yesterday was rather tiring." Oh? What happened? "I don't want to go into the details; after a while, each and every incident seems to blend into each other. Suffice to say that our daughter is a master manipulator, and that if I weren't a kitsune myself she'd have me wrapped about her little finger." Well, she is a fluffy kitsune... and they don't serve the Trickster for no reason. She should know as much. A sigh. "Oh, she's cute, and adorable, and fluffy, and nice to pet, and so on. And she knows that acting that way will considerably improve her chances of getting what she wants, even from me, so she does it all the time. Even when she's upset, our daughter can pout just so and still appear endearing... what's a mother to do when she has to instil some discipline in a wayward child?" She's starting to make Kinu sound like some kind of devious little vixen... "Oh, I'm pretty sure that she isn't acting all the time, but it's hard to tell when she's truly being endearing, and when she's just putting on an act. That's not the end of it, either — yesterday, [ kiyoko.numKits 4 |I caught her tricking one of her younger siblings into picking peaches for her..." Oh no. "Oh yes. 'Mama said I couldn't pick any of the fruit, but she didn't say anything about you doing it...' You can imagine what happened next. I had to spank the both of them quite soundly." |she tried to talk circles around me over dinner, trying to get me to replace her dessert with more kenchin soup. And I went to all that trouble to make such good daifuku, too..." You've heard of children wanting to swap their vegetables for dessert, not the other way around. "Dessert or not, it's improper to eat only things you like and leave out the rest or even worse, foist them onto others; I had to take her aside and drill that into her head." ] A regrettable but necessary decision. Kiyoko nods. "Look, I'm not trying to put down our prodigy of a daughter, but... don't get tricked, okay? I know the temptation is there to spoil Kinu as you don't get to be with her as often as you'd like, but don't let her fool you into doing what she wants all the time. I'd rather her not grow up to conform to every negative stereotype about us kitsune, and if she wants to be a den mother being childishly manipulative is not going to be a point in her favor." Okay, you understand. "Good." Kiyoko heaves in a deep breath, and exhales. "It's not that I don't love our children any less than when we started, but sometimes it's nice to have an adult to hold an intelligent conversation with at the end of the day. It makes me look forward to your visits." |You did have a question you wanted to ask... "Yes?" Where did Kinu's bell anklet come from? "Oh, I made it a couple of days after she was born. You reach across the table and give the kitsune mother a good petting between her big, fluffy ears. Kiyoko instinctively cranes her head forward to receive the affection, her jade-green eyes closing as she purrs gently. Now, then. It's understandable that she feels a little sad to see her daughter grow up, especially at such a young age and given the circumstances of the Astral Plane. But ultimately, the duty of a mother is to prepare her children for the day when they will no longer need her. Kinu may grow into someone greater than the two of you combined, but it's up to you and her — especially her, since you can't be around so often — to mold your daughter correctly and set her on the right path in life. Kiyoko looks away as you finish the petting, but doesn't say anything. There, there. |"Ehehe. Our daughter has really taken a shine to children. She seems to love her brothers and sisters more than I did when I was her age." Perhaps it's got something to do with the fact that unlike her mother, she doesn't have to deal with wailing fox kits and mountains of dirty diapers? "It's more than that, I think. She's just naturally good with her brothers and sisters and actually likes being put in charge of them; it's gotten to the point where I feel comfortable delegating important sibling-related responsibilities to her and know she'll carry them out with enthusiasm." A model big sister, then. Or maybe she just likes bossing around her siblings... while it's good that she's learning to wield authority at such a young age, even in a limited fashion, she needs to understand that this authority is to be wielded for the benefit of others, not massaging her own ego. Kiyoko looks thoughtful at that. "Come to think of it... hm. That explains a few things." Pardon? "Oh, it's nothing. But you're right — I should probably stress that bit of her education in responsibility a little more." ]"

rows.translation: 询问一下你的大女儿的情况。

rows.original: [kiyoko.numKits 1 2 4 8 16 24 32|[rand|"I'd be lying if I said I wasn't at least a little worried about the whole thing," Kiyoko admits. "I mean, for my tummy to swell up so quickly and my baby to grow into a child almost instantly... it's just not what I'm used to seeing. What does this place do to children? To me? Is it somewhere where I'd want to raise sons and daughters?" You pat Kiyoko on the shoulder and tell her that it's going to be all right. "I appreciate the sentiment, [pc.name], but the fact is that neither of us are sure of that." The kitsune flattens her fox ears against her head and rubs her temples. "Yes, I understand that there's little I can really do about the situation save do my best to raise Kinu well, but I'm not completely rational about this, you know?" Saying nothing, you continue to pat Kiyoko on the shoulder, slowly moving up to her head. It's all you can do to fight the melancholy creeping up on the usually peppy kitsune. "I mean, how much time have I lost without spending those years that I would've with our child as an infant? Sure, on the good side it means I don't have to deal with whole baskets of dirty diapers like I did for my brothers and sisters when they were young, but... well, babies have their moments. I really did like my siblings when they were babies; they were all so cute and fuzzy. "But listen to me go on like this, worrying about what I can't change. My situation's improved so much already, and all I can think about is how it might get worse. "I'd like to think I'm not one to scare easily, [pc.name]. But I do remember at least two times when I've been shaken to my core: first, when I realized I was trapped here in the Astral Plane, and secondly, when it hit home that I'm now responsible for more than just myself." |"I can't really decide whether Kinu takes more after me or you," Kiyoko says after some thought. "Little tyke's a kitsune all right, with the playfulness to match, but there's more to someone than their exterior, after all." Is kitsune blood that strong? Kiyoko shrugs. "I don't know. Never seen anyone breed with someone who wasn't a kitsune as well. And to be honest, even if I did, it's not as we did things the... um, conventional way, or at least in terms of what really happened." There's no need for undue worry, now. By all appearances, the daughter you and her made together is a perfectly normal and happy youngster. "I hope..." |"I suppose I'd better get to remembering all the things I used to do when Mother made me babysit my siblings. That knowledge is going to get put to use in good time." A gleam creeps into your eye. Oh? Kiyoko smiles, a warm, indeterminate smile that could turn naughty any moment. "Somehow, [pc.name], I get the distinct feeling that I'm not going to have the one and only kit to my name, thank you very much." Why, is that a divination she just made? A prediction of the future? And what are the odds on that, if she doesn't mind you asking? "Well, we diviners never say to be completely certain, but the chances of that are about as close to perfect as one can get." [kiyoko.pregStage 1|She rubs the rounded swell of her womb for emphasis. ] ] |[rand|So, how are the kids treating her? "You know how they say that two children aren't that much more work than one?" Not really, but it's an interesting saying. "Or how three aren't that much more work than two? Or how four aren't that much more work than three?" Yeah, you can see where this is going. "They have their good and bad days, and I have mine," Kiyoko continues with a sigh of resignation, then nods at you. "Like my own mother before me, I have to learn to take it all in stride. At least I've done this before, so I'm no stranger to juggling the care of several children." |"I've been drawing up a proper education for the children," Kiyoko tells you. "It's been hard to decide on an exact curriculum, but I hope to get things down soon enough." She's got to be a good teacher, isn't she? After all, she taught herself so many things while stuck on the Astral Plane. "Learning something yourself is one thing, imparting knowledge to another is something else altogether, although I won't say that there isn't overlap between the two. Thankfully, the children seem studious enough and willing to learn." They certainly take after their mother, then. "My main concern is practical real-life experience they'll need once you get us out of here," Kiyoko adds. "The forest beyond the hilltop might be endless, but in terms of variety it's actually very limited. I'd rather my sons and daughters not grow up stunted in that regard." |"To be completely honest, I'm quite thankful for the Astral Plane providing us with what we need," Kiyoko tells you after pausing to sip her tea. "Having so many of those needling little daily tasks done for you does make caring for a great number of children all the more possible." Yeah, you can see how leaving a dirty heap of clothes and finding fresh laundry in the cabinet would help. A nod. "Of course, I still assign chores; it took some working out, but I've got a good schedule going. Working the orchards, dusting and cleaning, cooking, making small repairs. I actually have to ask the plane itself to not fix those bits so the children can get to them, but I think it's a vitally important part of their education to realize that one day, not everything is going to fall into their lap when they want it." Living in a place which is pretty much as close as one can get to paradise... "Yes," Kiyoko says, finishing the thought for you. "It's a slow, painful death — if not of the body, then of the spirit. They won't suffer from crushing loneliness like I did, but it'll be an uphill battle to keep them from ending up utterly spoilt." Like how the Belharan Empire was just before its fall? Kiyoko wrinkles her nose daintily. "Something like that." ] |[rand|Her family's starting to get bigger these days, isn't it? Kiyoko wiggles her ears and smiles demurely at you. "Yes, it is. And I suppose I should thank you for that. I wasn't planning on this when I first made that proposal, and even for some time after I thought of the children as... by-products of your energy transferral. "Now, of course, I'm properly shamed for even entertaining such thoughts. Being a big sister is similar to being a mother in some aspects, but very different in others; I shouldn't have brought all of my expectations to the fold." From what you've seen of her, she's been the doing her utmost to be the best mother that she possibly can be. "I don't know about that, and even if it were true — well, is my best enough? But what I'm getting at, though, is that even though it has its ups and downs, this family that you've given me has been a source of constant joy in what ought to be this prison of mine. I can be grateful for as much." |"Not too long ago, I finished drawing up a system for putting some of the older children in charge of their younger brothers and sisters." Much like the one her own mother instituted, right? Kiyoko nods. "More or less. It worked rather well for me — after all, delegation is key everywhere, and a large family like this is no exemption. I only have so many hands and tails, after all!" And has it worked out well? "So far. At least this has been tried and tested, and I only need to step in when actual emergencies arise, instead of personally taking care of every single little chore and hiccup. How do you think I still get time to fold origami, do calligraphy and play the koto?" |"If you haven't noticed already, the cabin's begun to change." You think you have, but it's more and interior than an exterior thing, is it? Kiyoko shakes her head. "Remember, orbs of transference were created as weapons with which armies of kitsune were to be smuggled. The Astral Plane is perfectly capable of housing, feeding and otherwise providing for the needs of a literal army — and it changes itself to suit that fact." Right... "Whatever happens, we'll always be adequately provided for, so you don't have to worry about us. Focus on your efforts beyond this little realm." You will. ] |[rand|"You know how some women say they're turning into their mothers?" Yes, but they usually mean it in a derogatory sense, don't they? "Oh? And how do you know I don't mean it as such?" Aw, come on. You've been around her for long enough, known her in much more than one sense of the word... she didn't think that you wouldn't be able to read her, did she? That, and the fact that she's smiling in her oh-so-demure way. "I am?" She was. For being a servant of a trickster deity, she's not very tricksy. Nor very self-aware, either, which probably precludes the first. "No, I suppose not. But back to the point — to put it in a better light, at least I'm turning into the bits of my mother which I admired, and not the bits that I didn't, which is a small mercy. Perhaps it'd be better to say that I'm turning into an idealized version of my mother." Well, then. If that's what Kiyoko wants, you're not going to stop her. In fact, you hope that she surpasses her mother — something which you think she's well on the way to doing. "The compliment's appreciated." |You know... "Yes, [pc.name]?" Kiyoko sips at her tea. "A coin for your thoughts?" It's rather interesting as to how her figure hasn't deteriorated, but rather, improved with keeping. Having this many children would wreck most other womens' bodies. Kiyoko just shrugs and smiles ineffably, her ears twitching. "Most other women don't have their newborns grow into children at the breast, either. Or have their pregnancies progress this quickly. Or... well, you get the idea. The Astral Plane was never quite meant for long-term living on the scale of years, so strange things happen. I'm only grateful for this small mercy, you know?" Oh, definitely. Has she looked into the origins of this? She is a diviner, after all. "I think I did mention trying, but after losing all my leads I'm just content to take what's been given to me and not worry too much about what I can't change. I suppose if I'm going to have to look the part of a mother, I might as well be pleasing to the eye instead of the other way around, right?" No doubt about that! Kiyoko laughs. "Besides — and let's be honest here — can you visualize a fat kitsune? I don't think I can; Keros would never stand for it." |How goes the kits' education? Kiyoko practically beams at the question. "They're very talented, I swear; they seem to be able to pick up any skill or learning with much less effort than anyone else I'd know. Even with a century or two's worth of headstart on them, I'm sure it'd only take decades for them to catch up with me." That's marvelous! "I don't think this ability came from me, [pc.name], this affinity for learning. You seem to be able to pick up new knowledge and activities with relative ease compared to other people... almost as drastically as our children do. This is an ability the kitsune as a people would be very glad to have. "But I digress. I'm trying to do what I did for my younger siblings all that time ago — a well-rounded education, moreso now that I've the tools to do so. Mathematics, music, natural lore... although I will say that without a reference, history has been a bit of a bother. I try to frame it as a set of stories, rather than just dates and facts to be memorized — works better with the kits that way." You nod and gesture for her to go on. "A few of our children show some magical promise, so I'll see about that when they get older. When I eventually get out of here... when we do, that is, I want them to be useful to kitsune society. That's the ultimate goal of all this." As always, you're thankful for all her efforts in caring for your issue while you're away. "I'm just doing what a mother does, [pc.name]. Well, any respectable mother. There's no need to thank me at all — I'm just glad that all the things I learned to stave off boredom, to keep myself sane in this prison have actually turned out to have some use in the end." ] |[rand|"You know," Kiyoko says with a smile, "if I were out for good from this gilded cage of mine, I could very well be in the running for being a proper den matron." The name does suggest the qualifications, you suppose. Are you right? Kiyoko thinks a moment. "In a way. It's not strictly true that a den matron has to be the most prolific mother in the community — there's no rule stating as such — but once she gets the position she's pretty much propositioned by most of the males the den has to offer, and plenty others from other dens to boot. The mixing of blood is supposed to prevent excessive inbreeding, you see." Hrm. "Either way, if a den matron isn't one by the time she's named one, she'll be so in short order. As for me... well, I've enough children of my own that I could set up my own den all by myself." Better give her a few more, then. Can't have too many hands around to start striking the earth once she gets out of here. Kiyoko smiles sweetly at you and wiggles her large, fluffy ears, but says nothing. |"I'm glad all this has happened. Now, I'm still not very happy about being stuck in here for as long as I've been, and if I could I would have avoided it, but since it meant I got the opportunity to meet you and be a mother to so many children... it may just have been worth it." You're glad she thinks that way. All that's in the past now; there's a bright future ahead of her. Kiyoko nods. "To be able to see anything other than a perfect world... it's a relief. Perfection, especially when one has not earned it, is anything but. For the longest duration of my imprisonment here, I wanted for nothing, yet I had no reason to keep on existing as I was. I forced myself to pull through each day, each moment; I pretended to be excited that the highlight of my day was sitting down for hours on end and doing scroll painting... "But now, instead of living for nothing or even for myself, I've been given the opportunity to live for others. Instead of teaching myself to scroll paint for its own sake, I now teach the kits, and I learn as they do... to be given a meaning to exist, that's one of the greatest gifts both you and the children have bestowed upon me." You really didn't have such lofty goals in mind when you started making gifts of your chi to her. All you wanted was to - "Does it really matter why you did it? All that matters is that you did, and for that I'm grateful." Kiyoko closes her eyes and sips at her tea, and you see her lip tremble. "Please, continue doing what you're doing... and I'll work hard to support you from the rear." All right, you'll do just that. |"I think my mother would've been proud of me," Kiyoko says after some thought. "While I didn't quite become the famed diviner which she'd hoped for me to become by sending me off, I've nevertheless made something of myself." That can't be denied, yes. The Astral Plane sure has changed a lot ever since you first entered the place. "I think she'd have liked you too, [pc.name]. Then again, she liked anyone who was plenty virile, and I don't think you're lacking in proof of that." Kiyoko laughs and waves a hand dismissively. "At least you won't have to deal with any pesky in-laws in my case — chances are they're all dead by now." The world's changed since the Godswar by leaps and bounds. Even if she returned to her homeland once she's free, it's almost certain that it won't be as she remember it. "I don't know about that. Going back, I mean. It's far more likely that I'd ask the Trickster himself for permission to find someplace to settle and form a den in this locale. I think I've warmed up to the place some, and I'm sure he wouldn't mind having a presence around, no matter how small." ] |[rand|"I'd like to think I've gotten everything under control now," Kiyoko informs you, giving you a sagely nod as she picks a piece of candy off the plate. "At this point, most matters resolve themselves without my intervention, I've delegated most of the tasks to the eldest of our children, and I've raised them well enough to function without need for my constant oversight. I like to think I've succeeded as a mother in raising obedient, useful, and productive children, for what it's worth." She really is gearing up to be a den mother, isn't she? Kiyoko doesn't reply immediately, but stares out of the window for a second or two before finishing the last of her tea and licking her lips very, very slowly. "I suppose it's not too far off from actuality, is it? All that really remains is for Keros to give me his seal of approval; that's the only thing which is lacking. "But of course, it also means that I've more free time to do the things I truly enjoy, instead of dealing with endless squabbles and petty complaints. Things such as making more kits. Oh, there's no rush... but neither should one pause to rest on one's laurels, yes? There's always room for improvement." |How are the children treating her these days? By the looks of it, she's surpassed her mother several times over in terms of quantity. "Quantity, yes. Quality... well, I hesitate to make that judgement. My mother did produce me, after all — that's quite a hard achievement to top." Was that just a backhanded compliment she made there? Kiyoko just smiles. "But yes, to answer your question, [pc.name], the children are treating me just fine. By and large, they are respectful and obedient, with much potential for power... I don't want to venture guesses as to what came from which side of the family, but suffice to say that your seed and my womb work very, very well together." That's a polite way of putting it... but you are glad things have worked out well in the end. "Please, I do urge to continue. You and I... we're both doing very good work. It'd be a shame if either of us decided enough was enough." The kitsune dips her head ever so slightly and gives you a wink. |"Save for finally getting out of here on a permanent basis, I don't think there's anything else I could possibly ask for, [pc.name]. Ever since you arrived in my little world, the boons that have been granted to me are manifold — family, memories... and plenty of fun times. I know there're those who disdain the company of others, but when you've been to one extreme, it's hard to want to go back — I lost all my appetite for solitude after an eternity of it stuck in this gilded cage. "And speaking of cages... while I suppose I'm still imprisoned here, at least I don't mind it that much any more. Oh, I'd still like to get both myself and the orb fixed for the sake of the kits, but if it were up to me and me only... I don't think I care any more. Most people live bound in chains of their own making; even as I am, I think I'm considerably freer than most people are." It's a comfortable, idyllic life with the children, isn't it? Kiyoko nods. "Even afterwards... after my release... I still think I'd like to join you in your adventures, to project myself from the orb or even be with you in the flesh and offer you succor when you lay yourself down to rest. Even if physical distance separates us, there's no reason we can't meet in our dreams, there's no reason why you and I can't keep this arrangement going. I do find fighting alongside you rather... invigorating, plus I do get to test out the spells and abilities I devise. Plus, by this point, I'm not going to deny that I absolutely delight in receiving your chi and nurturing it within me, [pc.name]. Wouldn't have done it so many times if I didn't enjoy it, right? "So yes, don't worry about the kits and I; we're fine as we are. Focus your energies on the tasks which lie ahead of you... although if you have some left over for a faithful fox like me, I wouldn't be against taking some of that load off you."] |[rand|Kiyoko considers the question for a moment before setting down her tea and giving you a stupid, playful grin. "Even after all that we've been through, it still gladdens my heart every time you ask about the children. It's just — well — I just like hearing you pose the question." How many are there at this point, anyway? Sure, you've caught sight of some of the kits on the way in, but you'd never be able to count them all! Seventy-five? More? Who knows? "That's for me to know and for you to count." Well, if they could all assemble and stay in one place without zipping around all the time... "Trust me, these children don't have any setting besides off and full speed. I think they get that from their mother." |"The children and I are handling things very well. You know, when all of this started, I made a decision to try and recreate the system that my own mother used to have for managing me and my siblings, and it's worked out well. The children are cared for, fed, and given adequate love and attention. It's probably a little different from what you're used to, but the way I see things, there's no need to reinvent the wheel. If anything, I've made it even better." Oh? Kiyoko nods. "When a prospective den mother strikes out on her own, she doesn't do it alone; usually, several of her brothers and sisters come along for the ride. They help her take care of things and make the place suitable for little fox kits to grow up in. Of course, they add to their number, too, but most kitsune don't have the sheer —" you see Kiyoko run her tongue across her lips- "reproductive capacity a den mother does. I won't deny that the Astral Plane has been an immense help in this regard — it's nice to have a house that grows along with your family, not to mention the self-doing laundry. It gives me more time to tend to the children." And it also gives her more time to put towards adding to their number. "Ehehe..." Kiyoko tilts her head slightly and folds her ears forward. "I won't say no to playing with you, if that's what you want." |"The children and I couldn't be any better, thank you for asking. I haven't felt better in a long, long time, if ever, and the kits are all happy smiles all day. When I was new at this, I worried a bit as to whether I'd be able to give the kits all the attention they needed like my mother used to be able to do, but things just seem to have worked themselves out. I don't even need to think about things now, everything just falls into place of its own accord." Inasmuch the same way as she keeps on finding herself pregnant, right? "Exactly. You know what I'm talking about. Not that it doesn't require any effort on my part, but it's so enjoyable that it may as well not." Ah, to be able to do something you love for a living. Familiarity is supposed to breed contempt, but clearly that doesn't apply to your kitsune slut-wife and her enormous brood of children. "Sometimes they're quiet and calm, and sometimes they're running all over the place. At least their older brothers and sisters are well on the way to learning responsibility. They'll need it when we finally get out of here." Yes... "Like I said, I'm happy, and so are the children. Don't worry about us, and do what you need to do."] ]
rows.translation: [kiyoko.numKits 1 2 4 8 16 24 32|[rand|如果我说自己对这件事一点也不担心，那肯定是在撒谎。 清子承认了。 我的意思是，我的肚子会这么快就胀起来，而我的宝宝几乎瞬间就从一个婴儿长成了一个孩子……这种景象真的超出了我的想象。这个地方对孩子来说到底有什么影响？对我来说又是什么影响？这里真的是我想养育儿子女儿的地方吗？ 你轻拍着清子的肩膀，告诉她一切都会好起来的。 我很感激这种心意， [pc.name]但事实上，我们两人都不确定这一点。 那只狐妖将它的耳朵贴在头上，然后揉了揉太阳穴。 是的，我知道对于这种状况，我其实能做的并不多，只能尽自己最大的努力把绮奴抚养好。但你知道，我对此并不是完全理智的。 你什么也没说，只是继续轻拍着清子的肩膀，手部慢慢向上移，最终抚到了她的头。对于这个平时总是充满活力的狐妖来说，你能做的，就是尽自己最大的努力来抵抗那逐渐蔓延而来的忧郁情绪。 我的意思是，如果我没有把那些本该陪伴在孩子婴儿时期的时间花在别的地方，那我究竟错过了多少时轻型呢？当然，从好的方面来看，这也意味着我不用像照顾弟弟妹妹们小时候那样，每天都要处理一大堆脏尿布了，但是……嗯，婴儿时期也有它们独特的乐趣啊。我真的很喜欢我的弟弟妹妹们小时候的样子，他们一个个都那么可爱、那么惹人喜欢。 但是，你听听我这样不停地担心那些我无法改变的事情。我的情况其实已经改善了很多，可我满脑子想的却还是它可能会变得更糟。 我愿意认为自己不是那种容易受到惊吓的人 [pc.name]但我确实记得有两次经历让我深受震撼：第一次是当我意识到自己被困在了这个星界之中；第二次则是当我真正意识到，现在我不仅要为自己负责，还要为更多的人负责。 |我实在无法确定，绮奴更喜欢我，还是更喜欢你。 经过一番思考后，清子说道。 这个小孩子确实是一只狐妖，也确实有着与之相匹配的顽皮性格，但毕竟，一个人的本质并不仅仅取决于他们的外表。 狐妖之血真的有那么强大吗？ 清子耸了耸肩。 我不知道。我从没见过有人和不是狐妖的人交配。说实话，就算有人这么做过，他们的方式也不像我们……嗯，传统的那种方式，至少在某些方面是不一样的。 真的吗 发生了这样的事。 现在没有必要过分担心。从各方面来看，你们共同抚养的这个女儿，是一个完全正常且快乐的孩子。 我希望…… |我想我最好赶紧回想一下妈妈让我照看弟弟妹妹时我曾经做过的一些事情。这些知识以后肯定会有用处的。 你的眼中闪过一丝轻型芒。哦？ 清子笑了，那是一种温暖而难以捉摸的微笑，随时都可能变得调皮起来。 不知怎么的， [pc.name]我有一种强烈的感觉，那就是我无法拥有那套独一无二的装备了，真的非常感谢。
