rows.original: [rand|In the days before the empire, there existed a coven of witches who ruled much of the coastal lands beyond the sea. Their magic was strong and their rule absolute; life under their collective thumb could not be said to be terrible, but at the same time it could have been much better, too. As time wore on, intrigues and byplay began to bore these witches, and their gaze turned to lands beyond their borders with interest. While conquest grew to be their desire, none of them wished to partake of the risks such would involve; eventually, the coven hit upon the idea of creating a perfect warrior, a master strategist and tactician, skilled in every conceivable art of war. This perfect creature would go out and do battle in their name, while they sat in their palaces and reaped the rewards. So it came to pass that all the witches of the coven bent their minds to this task. Creating a human the usual way would take too long and leave too much to chance, so they fashioned with their magics an infant who was not born of any womb, but instead made. A homunculus, perhaps, yet far more than any simple construct, this boy was crafted in a cauldron of glass with the witches watching him every step of the process and making the necessary adjustments. And to control him and ensure he obeyed their will, the witches cocooned him with many threads of terrible fate, an ever-present sword ready to fall should he dare to defy his creators. Years dragged on. The infant grew into a boy, and the boy a young man of thirteen. Despite the magics used to extend youth and life alike, the witches were not growing any younger, and wanted to see results; in their haste, they sent their creation to skirmish along the northern border with a handful of troops. Understaffed and undersupplied, the boy did what he could, but was soon routed and the lad himself knocked into a ravine. When he came to, he found a girl sitting beside him in the ravine, perched on a rock. Horribly pale skin melded with her white hair, but most striking was the gray blindfold about her eyes. "Who are you?" the boy asked warily, for experience had unfortunately taught him to expect that women would make demands of him. "I am the Oracle of Tira," came the quiet, monotonous reply. "And my mistress has seen fit to free you from your fate. What is your name?" The boy could not give an answer, for the witches had bothered to give him even that small dignity. "Then you will be called Belhar," the oracle whispered, "And your flames will sear and mend alike as they bring harmony to the world." So it came to pass that the Oracle of Tira cut the newly-named Belhar from the doom that bound him, and created that most terrible thing that can ever befall any world: a man with no fate, a man whose decisions and choices truly matter, a man who can change the course of history by himself. And that was the beginning of their many adventures together, which are now told all across Savarra. |Perhaps someday, you will spot it. It takes many forms — a shop sandwiched between two others down the main street, where there was none before. Or perhaps it'll be a homely brick building by the side of the road. If you're lost in the forest or the mountains, it might be a simple thatched hovel, though sturdy in construction. Whatever it looks like on the outside, though, on the inside the shop will always be the same. The proprietor's name is Asche, and the jackaless wraps herself in white silk and golden paint. She always smells of sandalwood and jasmine as does her shop; though it's cramped and there are no windows, there's always enough light to see by, and the air is always fresh and free of dust. Asche greets all who enter her shop with the utmost politeness, and even though her accent and manner of speech may be foreign to some, no one even fails to understand her words. Mayhaps you are there merely to browse? Possible, but unlikely; few stumble upon Asche's Fanciful Trinkets by accident, and it's far more likely that you've been called to that place. People have problems, and what Asche sells are solutions... at a price. She is always upfront about what she wants. No hidden clauses, no tricks, no clever wordplay that leaves people paying far more than they'd bargained for. No, those are for her sister. Perhaps she'll want a letter delivered someplace. Perhaps she'll want your earliest memory. Other times, she'll ask for the sound of water rushing from mountain rapids. Who's to say? Nothing worth having ever came easy, after all. That doesn't stop some of her more unscrupulous customers from trying to cheat her or misuse her wares, but those never come to any good end. Asche has ways of ensuring that, yes. Today, it's there. Tomorrow, it's gone. Asche knows the value of being in the right place at the right time, and great fates can be sent rolling in the right direction with a mere nudge. The things that've come out of her shop have doomed great heroes and made kings out of kittens. When you see the place, the little shop, you'll know what it is. And why not step on in? So long as you deal with Asche fairly, she'll do the same with you. |Before the time of the Belhar Empire, there was a fertile valley which depended much on the river that flowed through it. Every spring, the river would flood, bringing with it fertile silt from within the heart of the mountains which made the valley rich and prosperous. Naturally, the river spirit was held in high honor in these lands. The sorcerers and witches who dwelt there said, "every year the river-goddess seeks a husband, who must be selected from among the people. If he is not found, then the river will not flood in the spring, and your harvest will be meager!" Then, when a boy came of age in some wealthy family, the sorcerers would say that he should be selected. Each time this happened, the unlucky parents would be forced to bribe them with large sums of money to look for someone else; the sorcerers would then order the rich folk to share the expense of buying some poor boy to be sacrificed to the river, keeping the rest of the money for themselves. But whoever would not pay, their son was chosen to be the husband of the river spirit, and was forced to accept the wedding gifts which the sorcerers brought him. The people of the valley chafed grievously under this custom, but feared the sorcerer and witches, who reputedly held much power. So it happened that one day Belhar and the oracle of Tira came to this valley, and heard of this wicked custom; together, they quickly devised a plan to put an end to it. Belhar came before the sorcerers and said, "I wish to be the river spirit's sacrifice this year. This way, no one's son will need to die; I am but a mere vagabond and my life is not worth much anyway." The witches and sorcerers were not pleased at first, but quickly reconsidered once it became known the valley's people were willing to pay large sums to have Belhar be sacrificed in their sons' stead. So when the day arrived, they gave him notice. Belhar dressed himself in the robes of ceremony the sorcerers had provided, climbed onto the palanquin and allowed himself to be carried to the riverbank. The elders of the people, as well as the sorcerers and the witches were all there, and from far and near men, women and children had flocked together in order to see the show. The sorcerers adorned Behlar with jewels and flower petals, and kettledrums, snaredrums and merry airs vied with each other in joyful sound. Now Belhar stood at the edge of the torrential waters, and was poised to leap in. But the oracle said, "don't be in such a hurry! Shouldn't everything be done solemnly and in order? Surely the river spirit will be glad to hear she has a new husband — won't one of you go and fetch her, so that she may come and receive him in state?" And with these words, the blind oracle turned to a witch and said in her quiet monotone, "you may go." The witch hesitated, so the oracle told Belhar to help her along her way by means of tossing her into the great river. Now it was clear the game was up. The sorcerers and witches began weaving their magics, but even the mightiest of mortals combined were no match for the oracle of time and death, let alone hedge-wizards who relied on deception and fear more than any actual power. Their spells shattered against Belhar and the oracle, and Belhar seized them one by one and cast the wicked sorcerers into the raging waters. Then Belhar declared to the people of the valley that the river-spirit had been merely a ruse to extort money from them, and that the Seven were the only gods who should be served. So it came to pass that the evil custom of appeasing the river spirit was at an end forever. ]
rows.translation: [rand|在帝国建立之前的那些日子里，有一群女巫共同统治着海洋彼岸的大片沿海地区。她们的魔法力量强大，统治也极为专制；在她们的统治下，人们的生活虽然不算糟糕，但同时也本可以过得更好。 随着时间的推移，这些女巫们开始对那些阴谋诡计和权谋手段感到厌倦，她们的目光开始转向边境以外的土地。虽然征服成为了她们的渴望，但没有人愿意承担随之而来的风险；最终，这个女巫团体想出了一个主意：创造出一个完美的战士——一个精通各种战争艺术的杰出战略家和战术家。 这种完美的生物会代表他们去战斗，而他们则坐在宫殿里享受胜利带来的回报。 于是，女巫们齐心协力完成了这项任务。用常规的方法创造一个人类需要太长时间，而且也会带来太多不确定性，因此她们运用魔法制造了一个并非诞生于母体的婴儿——而是通过其他方式诞生的。 制作完成或许他只是一个侏儒，但远不止如此——这个男孩其实是被女巫们用玻璃制成的。在整个制作过程中，女巫们始终密切注视着他的一举一动，并根据需要随时进行调整。为了控制他、确保他服从她们的意志，女巫们用无数条命运的丝线将他束缚起来；只要他敢违抗创造者的意愿，那把随时可能落下的剑就会立刻刺中他。 岁月悠悠，那婴儿渐渐长大，成了一个男孩，而这个男孩又长成了十三岁的少年。尽管女巫们使用了各种魔法来延缓衰老、延长寿命，但她们自己却并没有变得年轻起来。她们迫切地希望看到这些魔法带来的效果，于是便匆忙地将这个他们创造出来的少年派往北部边境，与少量军队一起参加战斗。 由于人手不足，物资匮乏，那个男孩已经竭尽全力了，但很快就陷入了困境，自己也不慎跌进了峡谷里。 当他恢复意识时，发现有个女孩坐在峡谷中的同一块岩石上，就在他旁边。 她那惨白的皮肤与白色的头发融为一体，但最引人注目的还是她眼睛上那块灰色的眼罩。 你是谁？ 男孩小心翼翼地问道，因为经验已经让他明白，女人往往会向他提出各种要求。 我是蒂拉的神谕者。 随之而来的是那声沉闷而单调的回答。 而我的女主人决定解救你，让你摆脱命运的束缚。你叫什么名字？ 那个男孩无法给出任何答案，因为那些女巫甚至没有剥夺他那一点点尊严。 那么你就会被叫做贝尔哈尔。 神谕低语道， 你的火焰既能灼烧，也能治愈，它们能为世界带来和谐。 就这样，提拉的神谕者将新被命名的贝尔哈尔从那束缚他的命运中解救出来，同时也创造出了世间最可怕的存在：一个没有命运的人，一个他的每一个决定和选择都真正具有意义的人，一个能够独自改变历史进程的人。 而这，正是他们共同开始无数冒险的起点，而这些冒险的故事，如今正在整个萨瓦拉地区广为流传。 |也许有一天，你会发现它。它的形态多种多样——可能是主街上那家之前并不存在的、夹在两家其他商店中间的三明治店；也可能是路边那座朴实的砖砌建筑。如果你在森林或山区迷路了，它可能会是一间结构坚固的简易茅屋。不过，无论它的外观如何，里面的陈设总是不变的。 这位店主的名字叫阿舍，她总是穿着白色的丝绸衣服，身上还涂着金色的颜料。她身上总是散发着檀香和茉莉的香气，她的店铺也是如此；虽然店铺空间狭小且没有窗户，但里面总是有足够的光线，空气也总是清新而没有灰尘。阿舍以极其礼貌的态度迎接每一位走进她店铺的人，尽管她的口音和说话方式对某些人来说可能有些陌生，但没有人会听不懂她的话。 也许你只是来浏览一下而已？也有可能，但可能性不大；很少有人会偶然发现“阿舍的奇趣小玩意儿”，更有可能的是，你被某种原因吸引到了那个地方。人们总是会遇到各种问题，而阿舍出售的，正是解决问题的方法……当然，这是需要付出代价的。 她总是直截了当地表达自己的需求。没有隐藏的条款，没有诡计，也没有那些会让人付出远超预期代价的巧妙言辞。不，这些手段都是她姐姐会用的。或许她只是想让人把一封信送到某个地方而已。 也许她会想要你最早的回忆；而有时候，她又会要求听到山间急流奔腾的声音。谁又能说得准呢？毕竟，任何值得拥有的东西，从来都不是一帆风顺就能得到的。不过，这并没有阻止那些不择手段的顾客试图欺骗她或滥用她的商品——但他们最终总是会自食其果的。 阿舍确实有办法确保这一点。 今天它还在那里，明天却已消失无踪。阿舍深知，在恰当的时间出现在恰当的地方是多么重要——只需轻轻一推，就能让伟大的命运朝着正确的方向前进。她店里出产的那些东西，有时会毁掉伟大的英雄，有时却能让小猫变成国王。 当你看到那个地方，那家小店时，你就会明白它的来历了。为什么不进去看看呢？只要你公平对待阿舍，她也会同样对待你的。 |在贝尔哈尔帝国建立之前，有一个肥沃的山谷，它的生存与发展在很大程度上依赖于流经其中的那条河流。每年春天，河水都会泛滥，将山脉深处带来的肥沃淤泥带入山谷，从而使这片土地变得富饶而繁荣。 自然而然地，在这片土地上，河灵受到了人们极高的崇敬。居住在那里的巫师和女巫们也这样说道 每年，河神都会寻找一位丈夫，而这位丈夫必须从人们中选出。如果找不到合适的人选，那么春天河水就不会泛滥，你们的收成也会十分稀少！ 每当某个富裕家庭中的男孩长大成人时，那些巫师就会建议选择他作为祭品。每次遇到这种情况，那些不幸的父母都不得不花费大量金钱去贿赂他们，以便他们能另选他人；而巫师们则会要求这些富人共同出资购买一个穷苦男孩来献祭给河流，然后把剩下的钱据为己有。 然而，那些拒绝支付的人，他们的儿子就会被选为河神的丈夫，被迫接受巫师们送来的结婚礼物。山谷里的居民对这一习俗感到极为不满，但他们害怕那些据说拥有巨大权力的巫师和女巫。 有一天，贝尔哈尔和蒂拉的神谕一起来到了这个山谷，听说了这种邪恶的风俗。他们立刻共同想出了一个办法来制止它。贝尔哈尔走到那些巫师面前，说道： 今年我想成为河神的祭品。这样，就不会有人的儿子需要死去；我只不过是个流浪者，我的生命本来也就没什么价值。 起初，那些女巫和男巫们并不乐意，但当他们得知山谷里的居民愿意支付巨额代价，让贝尔哈尔代替他们的儿子们被献祭时，他们很快就改变了主意。 于是，当那天到来时，他们通知了他。 贝尔哈尔穿上了巫师们准备好的仪式长袍，登上了轿子，由人们抬着他前往河岸。那里已经聚集了族人的长者们，还有巫师和女巫们；从远处到近处，男女老少们都纷纷前来观看这一盛况。 巫师们用珠宝和花瓣装饰着贝拉尔，而铜鼓、响鼓以及欢快的乐曲共同奏出了欢快的旋律。 此刻，贝拉尔站在湍急的水流边缘，准备纵身跃入水中。 但是神谕说道： 别这么着急！难道所有的事情不都应该有条不紊、庄重地进行吗？河神一定会很高兴听到她有了新丈夫的——难道就没有人去把她请过来，让她能够体面地迎接他吗？ 说完这些话，这位盲眼的先知转向一位女巫，用她那平静而单调的声音说道： 你可以走了。 女巫犹豫不决，于是神谕告诉贝尔哈尔，通过将她扔进那条大河来帮助她度过难关。 现在，一切都清楚了——这场游戏已经结束了。巫师们开始施展他们的魔法，但即便是最强大的凡人联合起来，也根本无法与这位掌管时间与死亡的神谕相抗衡，更不用说那些主要依靠欺骗和恐惧而非真正力量的边缘巫师们了。 他们的法术在贝尔哈尔和那位神谕者的面前纷纷失效，贝尔哈尔将那些邪恶的巫师一个个抓起来，扔进了汹涌的河水中。 随后，贝尔哈尔向山谷中的人民宣告：那条河之精灵只不过是他们用来骗取钱财的诡计，而真正的神明，只有那七位神明，才是人们应当崇拜的对象。 就这样，这种用来安抚河神的邪恶习俗永远地被废除了。 ]
rows.raw: " [rand|In the days before the empire, there existed a coven of witches who ruled much of the coastal lands beyond the sea. Their magic was strong and their rule absolute; life under their collective thumb could not be said to be terrible, but at the same time it could have been much better, too. As time wore on, intrigues and byplay began to bore these witches, and their gaze turned to lands beyond their borders with interest. While conquest grew to be their desire, none of them wished to partake of the risks such would involve; eventually, the coven hit upon the idea of creating a perfect warrior, a master strategist and tactician, skilled in every conceivable art of war. This perfect creature would go out and do battle in their name, while they sat in their palaces and reaped the rewards. So it came to pass that all the witches of the coven bent their minds to this task. Creating a human the usual way would take too long and leave too much to chance, so they fashioned with their magics an infant who was not born of any womb, but instead made. A homunculus, perhaps, yet far more than any simple construct, this boy was crafted in a cauldron of glass with the witches watching him every step of the process and making the necessary adjustments. And to control him and ensure he obeyed their will, the witches cocooned him with many threads of terrible fate, an ever-present sword ready to fall should he dare to defy his creators. Years dragged on. The infant grew into a boy, and the boy a young man of thirteen. Despite the magics used to extend youth and life alike, the witches were not growing any younger, and wanted to see results; in their haste, they sent their creation to skirmish along the northern border with a handful of troops. Understaffed and undersupplied, the boy did what he could, but was soon routed and the lad himself knocked into a ravine. When he came to, he found a girl sitting beside him in the ravine, perched on a rock. Horribly pale skin melded with her white hair, but most striking was the gray blindfold about her eyes. "Who are you?" the boy asked warily, for experience had unfortunately taught him to expect that women would make demands of him. "I am the Oracle of Tira," came the quiet, monotonous reply. "And my mistress has seen fit to free you from your fate. What is your name?" The boy could not give an answer, for the witches had bothered to give him even that small dignity. "Then you will be called Belhar," the oracle whispered, "And your flames will sear and mend alike as they bring harmony to the world." So it came to pass that the Oracle of Tira cut the newly-named Belhar from the doom that bound him, and created that most terrible thing that can ever befall any world: a man with no fate, a man whose decisions and choices truly matter, a man who can change the course of history by himself. And that was the beginning of their many adventures together, which are now told all across Savarra. |Perhaps someday, you will spot it. It takes many forms — a shop sandwiched between two others down the main street, where there was none before. Or perhaps it'll be a homely brick building by the side of the road. If you're lost in the forest or the mountains, it might be a simple thatched hovel, though sturdy in construction. Whatever it looks like on the outside, though, on the inside the shop will always be the same. The proprietor's name is Asche, and the jackaless wraps herself in white silk and golden paint. She always smells of sandalwood and jasmine as does her shop; though it's cramped and there are no windows, there's always enough light to see by, and the air is always fresh and free of dust. Asche greets all who enter her shop with the utmost politeness, and even though her accent and manner of speech may be foreign to some, no one even fails to understand her words. Mayhaps you are there merely to browse? Possible, but unlikely; few stumble upon Asche's Fanciful Trinkets by accident, and it's far more likely that you've been called to that place. People have problems, and what Asche sells are solutions... at a price. She is always upfront about what she wants. No hidden clauses, no tricks, no clever wordplay that leaves people paying far more than they'd bargained for. No, those are for her sister. Perhaps she'll want a letter delivered someplace. Perhaps she'll want your earliest memory. Other times, she'll ask for the sound of water rushing from mountain rapids. Who's to say? Nothing worth having ever came easy, after all. That doesn't stop some of her more unscrupulous customers from trying to cheat her or misuse her wares, but those never come to any good end. Asche has ways of ensuring that, yes. Today, it's there. Tomorrow, it's gone. Asche knows the value of being in the right place at the right time, and great fates can be sent rolling in the right direction with a mere nudge. The things that've come out of her shop have doomed great heroes and made kings out of kittens. When you see the place, the little shop, you'll know what it is. And why not step on in? So long as you deal with Asche fairly, she'll do the same with you. |Before the time of the Belhar Empire, there was a fertile valley which depended much on the river that flowed through it. Every spring, the river would flood, bringing with it fertile silt from within the heart of the mountains which made the valley rich and prosperous. Naturally, the river spirit was held in high honor in these lands. The sorcerers and witches who dwelt there said, "every year the river-goddess seeks a husband, who must be selected from among the people. If he is not found, then the river will not flood in the spring, and your harvest will be meager!" Then, when a boy came of age in some wealthy family, the sorcerers would say that he should be selected. Each time this happened, the unlucky parents would be forced to bribe them with large sums of money to look for someone else; the sorcerers would then order the rich folk to share the expense of buying some poor boy to be sacrificed to the river, keeping the rest of the money for themselves. But whoever would not pay, their son was chosen to be the husband of the river spirit, and was forced to accept the wedding gifts which the sorcerers brought him. The people of the valley chafed grievously under this custom, but feared the sorcerer and witches, who reputedly held much power. So it happened that one day Belhar and the oracle of Tira came to this valley, and heard of this wicked custom; together, they quickly devised a plan to put an end to it. Belhar came before the sorcerers and said, "I wish to be the river spirit's sacrifice this year. This way, no one's son will need to die; I am but a mere vagabond and my life is not worth much anyway." The witches and sorcerers were not pleased at first, but quickly reconsidered once it became known the valley's people were willing to pay large sums to have Belhar be sacrificed in their sons' stead. So when the day arrived, they gave him notice. Belhar dressed himself in the robes of ceremony the sorcerers had provided, climbed onto the palanquin and allowed himself to be carried to the riverbank. The elders of the people, as well as the sorcerers and the witches were all there, and from far and near men, women and children had flocked together in order to see the show. The sorcerers adorned Behlar with jewels and flower petals, and kettledrums, snaredrums and merry airs vied with each other in joyful sound. Now Belhar stood at the edge of the torrential waters, and was poised to leap in. But the oracle said, "don't be in such a hurry! Shouldn't everything be done solemnly and in order? Surely the river spirit will be glad to hear she has a new husband — won't one of you go and fetch her, so that she may come and receive him in state?" And with these words, the blind oracle turned to a witch and said in her quiet monotone, "you may go." The witch hesitated, so the oracle told Belhar to help her along her way by means of tossing her into the great river. Now it was clear the game was up. The sorcerers and witches began weaving their magics, but even the mightiest of mortals combined were no match for the oracle of time and death, let alone hedge-wizards who relied on deception and fear more than any actual power. Their spells shattered against Belhar and the oracle, and Belhar seized them one by one and cast the wicked sorcerers into the raging waters. Then Belhar declared to the people of the valley that the river-spirit had been merely a ruse to extort money from them, and that the Seven were the only gods who should be served. So it came to pass that the evil custom of appeasing the river spirit was at an end forever. ]"

rows.original: [rand|Long, long ago, in a world far removed from this one, there lived a race of bird-people known as the Avanai. Under the guidance of their patron goddess Stratos, who personally oversaw and guided the development of their civilization, the Avanai reached great heights of technological and magical knowledge, fueled in no small part by the secrets imparted by Stratos to her favored people. But then, their home world came under attack by an enormous host of nightmarish creatures, mindless misshapen entities born of the void between worlds with little desire save to be the anathema of all existence. Faced with this threat, the Grand Hierophant beseeched Stratos to extend her grace and mercy in aiding her chosen ones in stemming the tide of unmaking that threatened to consume their civilization. Naturally, she agreed. Thinking the Avanai having developed enough as a race to wisely use this knowledge, Stratos took the hierophant aside and taught him the greatest secret the goddess had been keeping for this moment: the method of creating life itself. Armed with this knowledge, the hierophant and his family labored to fashion this thing that his goddess had instructed him to build. His son shaped the construct's body, a man of stone, clay and crystal. His wife inscribed the hieroglyphs that contained the power of reason. His daughter taught its heart how to feel and experience the wonders of the world. And when they were done, the hierophant himself drew the symbol of Stratos on the construct's forehead and thereby imparted the Breath of Life upon this once inanimate creature. It worked, perhaps too well. Under the counter-assault spearheaded by the immense man of stone and crystal, the Avanai were able to drive back the void creatures long enough for the breach in reality to be mended, preventing them entry to their plane. Everyone rejoiced, and there was peace for a time. However, Stratos' help had come with one warning: that it was imperative that the golem be destroyed when its purpose was fulfilled, that her mark should be erased from it forehead when that time came. Yet the hierophant tarried — why should such a useful construct be demolished so quickly? There was always another building to be put up, another ditch to be dug, much rebuilding to be done now that the void creatures were gone. Surely the goddess would understand the need and grant her people a little grace. Just a few more days, and he'd rub out the mark on the golem's forehead. Yet as days dragged out into weeks, and weeks into months, the hierophant kept on finding reasons — no, excuses — to delay the golem's disassembly. And as more and more time wore on, the Avanai reported strange behaviors from the golem — making mistakes where it had previously followed orders perfectly, ignoring orders, staring into the distance. Yet even with these emerging behaviors, its great strength and hardiness was still so useful that the hierophant convinced himself to wait just a little longer. And then one night, when the hierophant was dining with his family, the walls on his home broke apart, torn asunder by his creation's gargantuan hands. He had not given the golem a mouth, yet it possessed one as it levelled its storm-filled gaze at him and spoke. "Build me a wife, for you have condemned me to eternal loneliness." At last, too late, the hierophant realized his mistake in ignoring his goddess' wisdom. Shouting for his family to flee, he wielded his magics and went forth to set right his error; creator and creation alike were destroyed in the battle that followed, along with much of the grand capital city of the Avanai. Today, the artificers of the Avanai still create automatons, imparting the Breath of Life to mere metal and crystal — ones that are far more advanced than that of the first golem to be fashioned. Yet three immutable laws have been set, to be disobeyed on pain of death: No creation shall possess the capacity to reason. No creation shall possess the capacity to feel. No creation shall possess the capacity to discern good and evil. Stratos had taught the hierophant how to create someone, yet the hierophant had treated it like something. |In Tychris where they honor Nareva above all the others of the Seven, there was a school in which one of the teachers was a monk. This particular monk was slothful in the extreme; there was nothing he loved more than to have a snack and a nap afterwards. Every morning before the lessons started, he ate so much that he could barely move; then soon after they began this lazy monk always took dozed off and slept until the bell for the end of the lessons sounded. The son of a poor villager was a student in the same school, and one day he asked the monk: "Teacher, may I ask you why do you sleep in all our lessons?" "My child," replied the monk without any embarrassment, "I merely appear to be sleeping; during these minutes I meet with Nareva in her Dream and listen to her wise words. That's why I try to sleep as much as I can." One time the student took care of his sick father during the night, and fell asleep at school in the morning. He slept so deeply that he didn't hear the bell, which woke the monk. When the monk saw the sleeping boy, he got very angry and took the student by the ear. "Ah, you little weasel! How dare you fall asleep in class?" "Teacher," replied the student, "I merely appeared to be asleep. I was with Nareva in her Dream and she taught me many truths about the world. Her domain was akin to a verdant garden temple, the white marble pillars standing tall and proud! Lush rose vines grew on them, all aflame with their red flowers, but none compared to the goddess' beauty as she spoke to me!" "And what," said the monk, snorting in disbelief, "did the great lady of knowledge, secrets and magic say to you?" "Well, one thing stood out amongst the knowledge she passed on: 'I must say, I've never had the dubious honor of receiving your teacher here.'" |After the passing of King Stephen the Brave, under whose wise and gentle rule the land flourished as it never had before, the crown passed to his second son — as the eldest had perished while hunting — whom history remembers as Robert the Foul. Robert was a winebibber and a whoremonger, quick to anger and slow to forgive, and he both impoverished the country with his profligacy and tormented the nobility and the peasantry with his cruelty, until at last a conspiracy of nobles brought the King's cup-bearer into their confidence, and they mixed the shavings of a poisonous mushroom into his wine. In the aftermath, before the coronation of Robert's successor, the nobles gathered together and considered what they could do to prevent the throne from falling again into such unworthy hands. And they reasoned that the Grand Duke, who had led the conspiracy against Robert the Foul, should take up this burden and swear a holy oath that if the king should fall into madness or wickedness he would take action against him and save the kingdom from his depredations. And as they made this decree, a hermit from the mountains of the east appeared at the door of their council chamber and asked them, "But what should happen if the Grand Duke himself becomes wicked?" And they answered that it was inconceivable that the Grand Duke should fall into wickedness, given the nobility with which he had acted against Robert the Foul and the illustriousness of his lineage, and they drove the hermit out with fists and curses. But it happened during the reign of Cedric the Meek, who was an unexceptional but well-respected king, that the Grand Duke conspired against him to take the throne for his own line. He invoked his ancient hereditary right to act against a wicked king and, naming invented crimes which Cedric had supposedly committed, which led a conspiracy of avaricious nobles to force out Cedric and put his own nephew on the throne. And what followed was a bitter civil war, in which the Grand Duke was only put down with greatest difficulty, and the kingdom was much dishonored in the eyes of its neighbors. In the aftermath, before the coronation of the Grand Duke's successor, the nobles gathered together and considered what they could do to prevent the Grand Duke from ever abusing his power to check the king. And they reasoned that the Archbishop, who had comforted the souls of those faithful to Cedric during the darkest times of the civil war, should take up this burden, and should rally all the forces of the Church against the Grand Duke should he ever overstep his role as the guardian of the king. And as they made this decree, a hermit from the mountains of the east appeared at the door of their council chamber and asked them, "But what should happen if the Archbishop himself becomes wicked?" And they answered that it was inconceivable that an Archbishop should fall into wickedness, given the fire of the Living Gods which was evident in his heart and the high office which he had attained, and the drove the hermit out with fists and curses. But it happened during the reign of James the Lesser that the King, the Grand Duke, and the Archbishop conspired together to tyrannize the nobles. They spent the royal treasury on fruitless wars against their neighbors, spilled the blood of their kin and countrymen with indifference, and suppressed every attempt to correct them, for each of them had been charged with the oversight of one of the others. And after the armies of the land were ground into dust, the remaining nobles made a pact with the merchants and craftsmen of the cities to overthrow the tyranny of the Triumvirate, though with great loss of blood and treasure. In the aftermath, with King, Duke, and Archbishop all executed and the honor of their offices thrown into disarray, they petty nobles and great men of the cites gathered together to proclaim a formation of a Parliament in which all men of noble character could come and cast their vote. And they reasoned that such a gathering of noble men could never fall into folly and treachery as the Triumvirate had, especially since it was the combined might of those classes which had forced out the wicked autarchs. And as they made this constitution, a hermit from the mountains of the east appeared and asked them, "But what should happen if the Parliament itself falls into wickedness?" And one of the eldest of the nobles, who had been a child during the reign of Cedric and remembered the counsel of the hermits from that time, asked the man, "Thrice you have troubled us with your warnings of failure when we have endeavored to preserve the future of the nation. Tell me, why do those of your order always appear at our door to warn us when we attempt to create a bulwark against the exercise of evil?" And the hermit answered, "Because you deceive yourselves when you think that evil is found in the form of government and not in the hearts of men. You set men to guard other men, and so increase the number of offices in which evil may take root. But this is folly: there is no constitution so noble that it will not be perverted should wicked men hold its offices." "Then what would you have us do to prevent the abuse of power by wicked kings, dukes, and archbishops?" "When evil men hold power, it is the duty of all righteous men to oppose them, and to seek their removal. But this duty cannot itself be made the charge of any title or office, for once you have done so, you have merely created another tool by which a wicked man may exercise his depravity under the guise of good. Even your noble selves may fall prey to this error." Thus the Parliament was incensed and drove the hermit out with curses and fists. But it happened thereafter that the nobles became indolent and self-possessed, and they ceased to look after the good of the commonweal, and the hearts of the merchants and the craftsmen were united against them, and prophets and demagogues arose in the cities and the countryside and stirred up the people to envy and wrath. And there followed the Time of Troubles, in which many were united for the overthrow of king and parliament entire, and others were united to protect their ancient privileges and customs. Terrible battles were joined, and provinces were burned, and terror overtook the streets of the capital, and the gutters ran with blood. And in the end the most radical and inflexible prevailed, and the privileges of suffrage were extended to all, and the hereditary Parliament was replaced with a universal democracy. And they declared that such a system of government could never fall into avarice and short-sightedness as the nobles had, for it was absurd to imagine that the will of the people themselves could fall into depravity. But when they signed the final acts of the new constitution in that hall where previously the nobles had joined each other against the wicked king, there was a silence that came over them, as if that place expected something which it remembered from generations past. But the silence went on and was filled by nothing except the chants of the revolution heard through the window, for the hermits of the east had all been killed in the Troubles, and their counsel was not heard in that place again. ]
rows.translation: [rand|很久很久以前，在一个与这个世界截然不同的地方，生活着一个被称为阿瓦奈的鸟人族群。在他们的守护女神斯特拉托斯的指引下——这位女神亲自监督并引导着他们文明的发展——阿瓦奈人在科技与魔法领域取得了惊人的成就。而斯特拉托斯向这些她所眷顾的族人传授的秘密，也在很大程度上推动了他们的进步。 然而，他们的家园世界遭到了大量噩梦般生物的攻击。这些毫无理智、形态畸变的生物诞生于世界之间的虚无之中，它们的唯一目的就是成为一切存在的诅咒。面对这一威胁，大祭司恳求斯特拉托斯施展她的恩典与慈悲，帮助她选中的人们阻止这场即将吞噬他们文明的毁灭浪潮。 她自然同意了。斯特拉托斯认为，阿瓦奈这个种族已经发展得足够成熟，能够明智地运用这些知识，于是他将那位祭司拉到一旁，向他传授了女神一直以来保守的最伟大秘密：创造生命本身的方法。掌握了这一知识，这位祭司和他的家族便开始努力制造出女神嘱咐他们要打造的那个东西。 他的儿子塑造了这个生物的身体，它是由石头、黏土和水晶构成的。 他的妻子在上面刻下了那些蕴含理性力量的象形文字。 他的女儿则教会了它的心如何去感受、去体验这个世界的奇妙之处。 当这一切完成后，那位智者亲自在它的额头上绘制了“斯特拉托斯”的符号，从而赋予了这个原本无生命的生物生命之力。 这一策略奏效了，或许效果甚至过于显著了。在那个由那位高大如石、晶莹如水晶的勇士所率领的反击行动中，阿瓦奈族人成功地将那些虚无生物击退，为足够长的时间赢得了修复现实中的裂隙、阻止它们侵入他们所在位面的机会。所有人都为此欢欣鼓舞，一时间，和平再度降临。 然而，斯特拉托斯的帮助附带了一个条件：当这个魔像完成它的使命后，必须立即将其摧毁，同时也要将其额头的标记彻底抹去。但那位祭司却迟迟没有采取行动——毕竟，这样一个如此有用的造物，为什么非要这么快就毁掉呢？ 总有另一座建筑需要建造，总有另一条沟渠需要挖掘，现在那些虚空生物已经消失，还有很多工作需要完成。女神肯定能够理解这种必要性，一定会赐予她的子民一些宽限。再过几天，他就能抹去那个魔像额头上的痕迹了。 然而，随着日子一天天过去，变成了几周，几周又变成了几个月，那位祭司不断找各种理由——不，是借口——来推迟拆解这个魔像。随着时间的推移，阿瓦奈人报告说这个魔像出现了许多奇怪的行为：那些它以前总是能完美执行的任务现在会出错，它还会无视命令，呆呆地望着远方。尽管出现了这些异常行为，但它强大的力量和坚韧的体质仍然非常有用，因此这位祭司说服自己再等待一段时间吧。 然后有一天晚上，当这位祭司与家人共进晚餐时，他家的墙壁突然被他自己创造出来的那个生物巨大的手爪撕得粉碎。他原本并没有给这个魔像配备嘴巴，但它却拥有了一张嘴，它用那充满暴风雨般的目光注视着他，然后开口说话了。 给我找一个妻子吧，因为你让我陷入了永恒的孤独。 终于，为时已晚，那位祭司才意识到自己忽视了女神的智慧，这是一个多么严重的错误。他大声呼喊让家人迅速逃离，然后施展法术去纠正这个错误。然而在随之而来的战斗中，无论是创造者还是被创造之物，都遭到了毁灭，阿瓦奈这座宏伟的首都城市也几乎被彻底摧毁。 如今，阿瓦奈的工匠们仍在制造自动机，他们将生命之力赋予那些仅仅由金属与水晶构成的机器——这些自动机比最初制造出的那个魔像要先进得多。然而，有三条不可违背的法则，违者将面临死亡： 没有任何创造物应当具备推理的能力； 没有任何创造物应当具备感知情感的能力； 没有任何创造物应当具备区分善恶的能力。 斯特拉托斯曾教导那位祭司如何创造这样的存在。一个然而，那位祭司却将其当作某种特别的东西来对待。东西. |在提克里斯，人们将纳雷瓦视为七位神明中最受崇敬的一位。在那里有一所学校，其中一位教师是一名僧侣。这位僧侣极其懒惰，没有什么比吃点心然后小睡一会儿更让他开心的了。 每天早上上课之前，他总会吃得很多，以至于几乎动弹不得；而课程一开始，这个懒惰的和尚就会打瞌睡，一直睡到下课铃声响起。 有个穷苦村民的儿子也在同一所学校上学，有一天，他问了这个和尚： 老师，我想问一下，为什么我们在上所有的课的时候您都在睡觉呢？ 我的孩子， 僧人毫不尴尬地回答道， 我只是 出现 在睡觉的时候；在那些几分钟里，我会在梦境中与娜雷瓦相见，聆听她那些智慧的话语。因此，我才会尽量多睡觉。 有一次，这个学生在夜里照顾生病的父亲，结果早上在学校里睡着了。他睡得太熟，根本没听到铃声，而正是这个铃声把僧人吵醒了。当僧人看到正在睡觉的男孩时，他非常生气，一把揪住了这个学生的耳朵。 啊，你这个小淘气！怎么敢在课堂上睡觉？ 老师， 学生回答道， 我看上去只是在睡觉而已。实际上，我和娜蕾瓦一起在她的梦境中，她向我揭示了许多关于这个世界的真相。她的领域就像一座绿意盎然的花园神殿，那些白色大理石柱子高耸挺立，显得如此庄严而美丽！茂盛的玫瑰藤蔓攀附在柱子上，红色的花朵竞相绽放，但没有任何东西能比得上女神在我身边讲话时的美丽与动人。 那么， 那位僧人难以置信地哼了一声，说道， 那位掌握知识、秘密与魔法的伟大女性，有没有对你说过什么吗？ 嗯，在她传授给我的知识中，有那么一点特别引人注意：‘我必须承认，我从未有幸成为你的老师。 |在勇敢的斯蒂芬国王去世后，在他的明智而仁慈的统治下，这片土地迎来了前所未有的繁荣。王位传给了他的次子——因为长子在狩猎中不幸身亡——历史将这位国王称为“邪恶的罗伯特”。 罗伯特是个酒鬼，也是个好色之徒，他容易发怒，也很难原谅别人。他的挥霍无度使国家陷入贫困，而他的残忍行为更是让贵族和平民都深受折磨。最终，一些贵族密谋策划，让国王的酒侍取得了他们的信任，于是他们在他的酒中掺入了有毒的蘑菇碎片。 在罗伯特的继任者加冕之前，贵族们聚集在一起，商讨该如何阻止王位再次落入如此不配的人手中。他们认为，那位曾领导阴谋反对罗伯特的大公，应该承担这一责任，发下神圣的誓言：如果国王陷入疯狂或邪恶，他就必须采取行动来阻止他，拯救王国免受其破坏。 就在他们颁布这项法令的时候，一位来自东部山区的隐士出现在他们的会议厅门口，向他们提出了这个问题。 但是，如果大公本人也变得邪恶起来，那该怎么办呢？ 他们回答说，考虑到大公在对抗“肮脏的罗伯特”时所表现出的高尚品质，以及他那显赫的家族背景，他竟然会堕入邪恶之中，这种想法简直是不可想象的。于是，他们用拳头和咒骂将那位隐士赶了出去。 然而，这件事发生在温和的塞德里克统治时期。塞德里克虽然并非一位杰出的国王，但却深受民众的尊敬。这时，大公密谋反对他，企图为自己的家族夺取王位。大公援引自己世代相传的权力，以塞德里克犯下的所谓罪行为借口，煽动了一群贪图权力的贵族们共同参与这场阴谋。最终，这些贵族们迫使塞德里克退位，将自己的侄子推上了王位。 随后爆发了一场残酷的内战，最终才以巨大的代价才将大公制服，而这个王国也因此在邻国眼中失去了应有的尊严。 在这一切发生之后，在大公的继任者加冕之前，贵族们聚集在一起，商讨该如何阻止大公滥用权力来制约国王。他们认为，那位在内战最黑暗的时期为那些忠于塞德里克的人提供精神慰藉的大主教，应该承担这一责任——如果大公超越了作为国王守护者的职责，就应该动员教会的所有力量来对抗他。 就在他们颁布这项法令的时候，一位来自东部山区的隐士出现在他们的会议厅门口，向他们提出了这个问题。 但是，如果大主教本人也变得邪恶了呢？ 他们回答说，考虑到这位大主教心中怀有活神赐予的力量，以及他所担任的高位，他竟然会堕入邪恶之中，这是根本无法想象的。于是，他们用拳头和咒骂将那位隐士赶了出去。 然而，就在小詹姆斯统治期间，国王、大公和大主教联手压迫贵族们。他们将王室财库用于与邻国的无谓战争，冷漠地践踏同胞的生命，同时镇压一切试图纠正他们行为的努力——因为这三个人各自都负责监督另外两人的行为。 当那些地方的军队被彻底消灭之后，剩下的贵族们与城里的商人们和工匠们结成了联盟，共同推翻了三头政治的暴政——尽管这一过程付出了巨大的鲜血和财富代价。 事态发展之后，随着国王、公爵和大主教的相继被处决，他们所担任的职位也彻底失去了原有的尊严与权威，那些小贵族以及城中的显要人物便聚在一起，宣布成立一个议会，让所有品行高尚的人都能参与投票。他们认为，这样的贵族集会绝对不会像三头同盟那样陷入愚蠢和背叛之中，更何况正是这些贵族阶层的联合力量，才迫使那些邪恶的统治者退位。 就在他们制定这份宪法的时候，一位来自东部山区的隐士出现了，他向他们提出了这个问题。 但是，如果议会本身也陷入了邪恶之中，那该怎么办呢？ 在塞德里克统治时期还是个孩子的那些贵族中，有一位年纪最大的人记得当时隐士们给出的建议，他便向那个人提出了这个问题。 在我们为守护国家的未来而努力时，你们已经三次因为那些关于失败的警告来打扰我们。告诉我，为什么每当我们试图抵御邪恶的力量时，你们的人总是会出现在我们的面前提醒我们呢？ 隐士回答道， 因为当你们认为邪恶存在于政府的形式之中，而非人们的内心时，其实你们是在自欺欺人。你们让人们去监视其他人，这样一来，那些可能滋生邪恶的职位数量也就增加了。但这种做法实在愚蠢——没有任何一部宪法是如此高尚，以至于当邪恶之人担任这些职位时，它就不会被扭曲。 那么，你们希望我们采取什么措施来防止邪恶的国王、公爵和大主教滥用权力呢？ 当恶人掌权时，所有正义之人的责任就是反对他们，并努力将他们赶下台。然而，这一责任本身不应成为任何头衔或职位的象征，因为一旦你将这一责任与特定的头衔或职位联系起来，你就只会为恶人提供一种新的工具，让他们能够以正义的名义继续行恶。即便是你们这些高尚的人，也可能会犯这种错误。 于是，议会勃然大怒，用咒骂和拳头将那位隐士赶了出去。 然而此后，贵族们变得懒惰而自以为是，他们不再关心公共利益，商人和工匠们也联合起来反对他们。在城市和乡村中，先知和煽动者们出现，他们激发人们的嫉妒与愤怒。 随后便是动乱时期。许多人联合起来，企图推翻国王和整个议会；而另一些人则团结一致，誓死捍卫他们世代相传的特权与习俗。激烈的战斗接连不断，各个省份相继被焚毁，首都的街道上充满了恐怖与杀戮，阴沟里也流淌着鲜血。 最终，最激进、最固执的观点取得了胜利，选举权被扩展到了所有人，世袭的议会也被普遍民主制度所取代。他们宣称，这样的政府体制永远不会像贵族们那样陷入贪婪与短视，因为认为人民的意志也会堕落，这种想法本身就是荒谬的。 但当他们在那个曾经是贵族们联合起来反抗邪恶国王的地方签署新宪法的最后文件时，一种寂静笼罩了他们，仿佛那个地方期待着某些自远古时代就铭记在心的东西。然而，这种寂静持续着，除了窗外传来的革命口号声之外，再没有任何其他声音。因为东方的隐士们都在那些动乱中丧生了，他们的智慧再也没有在这个地方被人们倾听。 ]
rows.raw: ' [rand|Long, long ago, in a world far removed from this one, there lived a race of bird-people known as the Avanai. Under the guidance of their patron goddess Stratos, who personally oversaw and guided the development of their civilization, the Avanai reached great heights of technological and magical knowledge, fueled in no small part by the secrets imparted by Stratos to her favored people. But then, their home world came under attack by an enormous host of nightmarish creatures, mindless misshapen entities born of the void between worlds with little desire save to be the anathema of all existence. Faced with this threat, the Grand Hierophant beseeched Stratos to extend her grace and mercy in aiding her chosen ones in stemming the tide of unmaking that threatened to consume their civilization. Naturally, she agreed. Thinking the Avanai having developed enough as a race to wisely use this knowledge, Stratos took the hierophant aside and taught him the greatest secret the goddess had been keeping for this moment: the method of creating life itself. Armed with this knowledge, the hierophant and his family labored to fashion this thing that his goddess had instructed him to build. His son shaped the construct's body, a man of stone, clay and crystal. His wife inscribed the hieroglyphs that contained the power of reason. His daughter taught its heart how to feel and experience the wonders of the world. And when they were done, the hierophant himself drew the symbol of Stratos on the construct's forehead and thereby imparted the Breath of Life upon this once inanimate creature. It worked, perhaps too well. Under the counter-assault spearheaded by the immense man of stone and crystal, the Avanai were able to drive back the void creatures long enough for the breach in reality to be mended, preventing them entry to their plane. Everyone rejoiced, and there was peace for a time. However, Stratos' help had come with one warning: that it was imperative that the golem be destroyed when its purpose was fulfilled, that her mark should be erased from it forehead when that time came. Yet the hierophant tarried — why should such a useful construct be demolished so quickly? There was always another building to be put up, another ditch to be dug, much rebuilding to be done now that the void creatures were gone. Surely the goddess would understand the need and grant her people a little grace. Just a few more days, and he'd rub out the mark on the golem's forehead. Yet as days dragged out into weeks, and weeks into months, the hierophant kept on finding reasons — no, excuses — to delay the golem's disassembly. And as more and more time wore on, the Avanai reported strange behaviors from the golem — making mistakes where it had previously followed orders perfectly, ignoring orders, staring into the distance. Yet even with these emerging behaviors, its great strength and hardiness was still so useful that the hierophant convinced himself to wait just a little longer. And then one night, when the hierophant was dining with his family, the walls on his home broke apart, torn asunder by his creation's gargantuan hands. He had not given the golem a mouth, yet it possessed one as it levelled its storm-filled gaze at him and spoke. "Build me a wife, for you have condemned me to eternal loneliness." At last, too late, the hierophant realized his mistake in ignoring his goddess' wisdom. Shouting for his family to flee, he wielded his magics and went forth to set right his error; creator and creation alike were destroyed in the battle that followed, along with much of the grand capital city of the Avanai. Today, the artificers of the Avanai still create automatons, imparting the Breath of Life to mere metal and crystal — ones that are far more advanced than that of the first golem to be fashioned. Yet three immutable laws have been set, to be disobeyed on pain of death: No creation shall possess the capacity to reason. No creation shall possess the capacity to feel. No creation shall possess the capacity to discern good and evil. Stratos had taught the hierophant how to create someone, yet the hierophant had treated it like something. |In Tychris where they honor Nareva above all the others of the Seven, there was a school in which one of the teachers was a monk. This particular monk was slothful in the extreme; there was nothing he loved more than to have a snack and a nap afterwards. Every morning before the lessons started, he ate so much that he could barely move; then soon after they began this lazy monk always took dozed off and slept until the bell for the end of the lessons sounded. The son of a poor villager was a student in the same school, and one day he asked the monk: "Teacher, may I ask you why do you sleep in all our lessons?" "My child," replied the monk without any embarrassment, "I merely appear to be sleeping; during these minutes I meet with Nareva in her Dream and listen to her wise words. That's why I try to sleep as much as I can." One time the student took care of his sick father during the night, and fell asleep at school in the morning. He slept so deeply that he didn't hear the bell, which woke the monk. When the monk saw the sleeping boy, he got very angry and took the student by the ear. "Ah, you little weasel! How dare you fall asleep in class?" "Teacher," replied the student, "I merely appeared to be asleep. I was with Nareva in her Dream and she taught me many truths about the world. Her domain was akin to a verdant garden temple, the white marble pillars standing tall and proud! Lush rose vines grew on them, all aflame with their red flowers, but none compared to the goddess' beauty as she spoke to me!" "And what," said the monk, snorting in disbelief, "did the great lady of knowledge, secrets and magic say to you?" "Well, one thing stood out amongst the knowledge she passed on: 'I must say, I've never had the dubious honor of receiving your teacher here.'" |After the passing of King Stephen the Brave, under whose wise and gentle rule the land flourished as it never had before, the crown passed to his second son — as the eldest had perished while hunting — whom history remembers as Robert the Foul. Robert was a winebibber and a whoremonger, quick to anger and slow to forgive, and he both impoverished the country with his profligacy and tormented the nobility and the peasantry with his cruelty, until at last a conspiracy of nobles brought the King's cup-bearer into their confidence, and they mixed the shavings of a poisonous mushroom into his wine. In the aftermath, before the coronation of Robert's successor, the nobles gathered together and considered what they could do to prevent the throne from falling again into such unworthy hands. And they reasoned that the Grand Duke, who had led the conspiracy against Robert the Foul, should take up this burden and swear a holy oath that if the king should fall into madness or wickedness he would take action against him and save the kingdom from his depredations. And as they made this decree, a hermit from the mountains of the east appeared at the door of their council chamber and asked them, "But what should happen if the Grand Duke himself becomes wicked?" And they answered that it was inconceivable that the Grand Duke should fall into wickedness, given the nobility with which he had acted against Robert the Foul and the illustriousness of his lineage, and they drove the hermit out with fists and curses. But it happened during the reign of Cedric the Meek, who was an unexceptional but well-respected king, that the Grand Duke conspired against him to take the throne for his own line. He invoked his ancient hereditary right to act against a wicked king and, naming invented crimes which Cedric had supposedly committed, which led a conspiracy of avaricious nobles to force out Cedric and put his own nephew on the throne. And what followed was a bitter civil war, in which the Grand Duke was only put down with greatest difficulty, and the kingdom was much dishonored in the eyes of its neighbors. In the aftermath, before the coronation of the Grand Duke's successor, the nobles gathered together and considered what they could do to prevent the Grand Duke from ever abusing his power to check the king. And they reasoned that the Archbishop, who had comforted the souls of those faithful to Cedric during the darkest times of the civil war, should take up this burden, and should rally all the forces of the Church against the Grand Duke should he ever overstep his role as the guardian of the king. And as they made this decree, a hermit from the mountains of the east appeared at the door of their council chamber and asked them, "But what should happen if the Archbishop himself becomes wicked?" And they answered that it was inconceivable that an Archbishop should fall into wickedness, given the fire of the Living Gods which was evident in his heart and the high office which he had attained, and the drove the hermit out with fists and curses. But it happened during the reign of James the Lesser that the King, the Grand Duke, and the Archbishop conspired together to tyrannize the nobles. They spent the royal treasury on fruitless wars against their neighbors, spilled the blood of their kin and countrymen with indifference, and suppressed every attempt to correct them, for each of them had been charged with the oversight of one of the others. And after the armies of the land were ground into dust, the remaining nobles made a pact with the merchants and craftsmen of the cities to overthrow the tyranny of the Triumvirate, though with great loss of blood and treasure. In the aftermath, with King, Duke, and Archbishop all executed and the honor of their offices thrown into disarray, they petty nobles and great men of the cites gathered together to proclaim a formation of a Parliament in which all men of noble character could come and cast their vote. And they reasoned that such a gathering of noble men could never fall into folly and treachery as the Triumvirate had, especially since it was the combined might of those classes which had forced out the wicked autarchs. And as they made this constitution, a hermit from the mountains of the east appeared and asked them, "But what should happen if the Parliament itself falls into wickedness?" And one of the eldest of the nobles, who had been a child during the reign of Cedric and remembered the counsel of the hermits from that time, asked the man, "Thrice you have troubled us with your warnings of failure when we have endeavored to preserve the future of the nation. Tell me, why do those of your order always appear at our door to warn us when we attempt to create a bulwark against the exercise of evil?" And the hermit answered, "Because you deceive yourselves when you think that evil is found in the form of government and not in the hearts of men. You set men to guard other men, and so increase the number of offices in which evil may take root. But this is folly: there is no constitution so noble that it will not be perverted should wicked men hold its offices." "Then what would you have us do to prevent the abuse of power by wicked kings, dukes, and archbishops?" "When evil men hold power, it is the duty of all righteous men to oppose them, and to seek their removal. But this duty cannot itself be made the charge of any title or office, for once you have done so, you have merely created another tool by which a wicked man may exercise his depravity under the guise of good. Even your noble selves may fall prey to this error." Thus the Parliament was incensed and drove the hermit out with curses and fists. But it happened thereafter that the nobles became indolent and self-possessed, and they ceased to look after the good of the commonweal, and the hearts of the merchants and the craftsmen were united against them, and prophets and demagogues arose in the cities and the countryside and stirred up the people to envy and wrath. And there followed the Time of Troubles, in which many were united for the overthrow of king and parliament entire, and others were united to protect their ancient privileges and customs. Terrible battles were joined, and provinces were burned, and terror overtook the streets of the capital, and the gutters ran with blood. And in the end the most radical and inflexible prevailed, and the privileges of suffrage were extended to all, and the hereditary Parliament was replaced with a universal democracy. And they declared that such a system of government could never fall into avarice and short-sightedness as the nobles had, for it was absurd to imagine that the will of the people themselves could fall into depravity. But when they signed the final acts of the new constitution in that hall where previously the nobles had joined each other against the wicked king, there was a silence that came over them, as if that place expected something which it remembered from generations past. But the silence went on and was filled by nothing except the chants of the revolution heard through the window, for the hermits of the east had all been killed in the Troubles, and their counsel was not heard in that place again. ]'

rows.original: [rand|It could never be said that Gunther Tovaldssen was anyone of note. Mostly, he led a simple, fulfilled life — a taciturn dog of the snow and woods, stoic save for a quick temper but skilled and quick of decision, reliant enough to be considered a hound dog worth following. The woods leading from the Governor's palace to the eastern coast were rich and bountiful, and like his ancestors before him, Gunther took what he needed from the ancestral lands that belonged to no lupine, and defended his family longhouse from the things that came down from the mountains. Alas, it was desire that undid Gunther. Not for riches or fame, but for something that would appeal to the simple hound that he once was — the forests of the ancestral lands were said to hold a fabled white hart, a one-of-a-kind creature only brought down in legend by the Jarls of old. With a pelt as white as snow and eyes of blazing green, this fabled creature stalked the woods that lupines had hunted in for generations — and the Belharan governor now claimed as his own private reserve. Those were the days when the Old Wyld superseded any law of man, and in either case Gunther reasoned that no ruler, let alone one who hid indoors out of the cold, should have claim to such profound majesty. In direct defiance of the governor's edicts, he stalked the pines and oaks from dusk till dawn, searching, waiting — until the day of the full moon, when the magnificent creature revealed itself and his javelin struck home. The next night, Gunther and the kin of his pack feasted upon the sweet flesh of the hart, its head and pelt occupying a place of honor upon his mantle. For half the night, Gunther was a hero. For the other half, he was a terror. Determined to make an example of this criminal to cement his already shaky rule, the Belharan governor had mustered his soldiers outside the little lupine hamlet. Those who came out to fight were cut down by the phalanxes; those who hid indoors were barred in their longhouses and set ablaze. Gunther himself fought, bringing down five belharans with shortsword and javelin alike, but was brought down by a lethal wound to the gut, the last moments of his life being the sight of his intestines spilling onto the ground. He should have died; the world would have been a better place. But somewhere in the void between life and death, a sinister whisper reached into Gunther's mind and offered him his heart's desire... his soul in exchange for power, and his body to use as a vessel. The deal was quickly struck; where once Gunther hunted to live, now he lived to hunt. Today, the wraiths are gone, defeated, and Belhar itself is but a pale shadow of what it used to be. Yet the thing that Gunther once was stalks field and forest, fjord and fall, refusing to die until the last traces of Belhar have been wiped from the face of the world, until it has not just merely passed, but as if the empire never had been. Should you lose your way in the wilderness, approach his campfire with caution; he will greet you in friendship, and share what meager food he has, but let him smell the taint of belhar upon you and your life is forfeit. |Once upon a time, there was a lake on the peak of the highest mountain in all of Savarra, and all kinds of plants grew around it. The plants flourished, and each one produced its own flowers, but in the first days of our world the blossoms had neither scent nor color. However, the water had within it all the colors of the rainbow, and gave off pleasant fragrances that changed from moment to moment. One day, the water asked the flowering plants, "wouldn't you like to have colors and fragrances of your own?" "Yes, yes!" the plants replied eagerly. "We would love to have flowers like that; please share your beautiful colors and sweet scents with us." "Then at midnight tonight, drop one of your flowers into the lake," the water replied. "Make a wish for the color and fragrance you would like." Precisely at midnight, the flowering plants dropped one flower each into the enchanted lake, and made their wishes. Some of them chose beautiful colors and sweet scents, and it was fine for them. Some had chosen lovely colors, but forgotten to pick a scent, while the opposite was true for others. Yet others had picked unpleasant scents by mistake, because having no experience of such matters, they had chosen what they had thought would be fitting, but was in actuality not so. Perhaps the most unfortunate ones who had not heard what was happening and slept through the night; they lost the opportunity to choose and hence have flowers without color or scent. And that is how all the flowers in the world came to have the scents and colors they have today. ]
rows.translation: [rand|根本不能说冈瑟·托瓦尔德森是个什么了不起的人物。他过着简单而充实的生活——就像一只沉默寡言的雪地森林之犬，虽然脾气有些急躁，但行事果断、能力出众，因此完全可以被视为一只值得追随的猎犬。 从总督府通往东海岸的那些森林里资源丰富，物产充沛。和他的祖先们一样，冈瑟从这片不属于任何人的祖传土地上获取他所需要的资源，同时保护着自己的家族住所，免受从山上袭来的各种威胁。 唉，正是欲望毁了冈瑟。他追求的并非财富或名声，而是那些能触动他内心深处原始渴望的东西——据说祖先的土地上蕴藏着传说中的白色雄鹿，这种独一无二的生物只有古代的贵族们才能猎获。它有着如雪般洁白的皮毛和燃烧般的绿色眼睛，这种神秘的生物在那些狼族世代狩猎的森林中出没，而现在的贝拉兰总督却将这些森林据为己有，当作自己的私人领地。 那些日子里，古老的荒野完全凌驾于人类的法律之上。冈瑟认为，任何统治者——更不用说那些因为寒冷而躲在室内的人——都无权拥有如此崇高的威严。他公然违抗总督的法令，从黄昏走到黎明，在松树林和橡树林中搜寻、等待——直到满月之夜，那个庄严而强大的生物终于现身，而他的标枪也精准地击中了目标。 第二天晚上，冈瑟和他的同伴们享用了那头雄鹿美味的肉，它的头和皮毛还被他珍藏在自己的斗篷上。 整个夜晚，冈瑟都像一位英雄一样行事；而到了后半段，他却变成了一个恐怖的存在。为了给这个罪犯一个教训，从而巩固自己本就摇摇欲坠的统治地位，贝拉兰的统治者召集了他的士兵们，来到了那个位于狼群出没的小村庄之外。 那些出来战斗的人被方阵士兵们击倒；而那些躲在室内的人则被关在长屋里然后被放火焚烧。冈瑟本人也参与了战斗，他用短剑和标枪接连击倒了五名贝拉人，但最终还是因腹部受到致命伤而倒下，在生命的最后时刻，他亲眼看到自己的肠子洒落在地上。 他本应该死去，那样这个世界才会变得更好。但在生与死之间的虚无之中，有一个阴险的低语进入了冈瑟的脑海，向他提供了他内心最渴望的东西……用他的灵魂换取力量，用他的身体作为载体。这个交易很快就达成了；从前冈瑟是为了生存而狩猎，现在，他则是为了狩猎而活着。 如今，那些幽灵早已被消灭，贝尔哈尔也只不过是它昔日辉煌的苍白残影。然而，冈瑟曾经拥有的那股力量仍在田野、森林、峡湾与山谷中游荡，不肯消逝——直到贝尔哈尔的最后痕迹从这个世界上彻底消失，直到这个帝国仿佛从未存在过一样。 如果你在荒野中迷路了，一定要小心地靠近他的篝火；他会以友好的态度迎接你，并与你分享他那为数不多的食物。但是，如果让他察觉到你身上有贝尔哈尔的气息，你的性命就会不保。 |从前，在萨瓦拉最高的山顶上有一个湖泊，周围生长着各种各样的植物。这些植物茁壮成长，每一株都开出了自己的花朵，但在我们这个世界的最初时期，这些花朵既没有香味也没有颜色。然而，湖水却蕴含着彩虹般的各种色彩，并散发出令人愉悦的芬芳，这些芬芳会时刻发生变化。 有一天，湖水问那些开花的植物们 你难道不想要属于自己的颜色和香味吗？ 是的，是的！ 这些植物立刻做出了回应。 我们也很想要这样的花朵；请将你们美丽的色彩和芬芳的气息与我们分享吧。 那么就在今晚午夜时分，把你的花中的一朵扔进湖里吧。 水作出了回应。 许一个关于你想要的颜色和香气的愿望吧。 正值午夜时分，这些开花植物各自将一朵花投入那片被施了魔法的湖中，许下了自己的愿望。有些植物选择了美丽的颜色和甜美的香气，这样当然很好；有些则选了漂亮的色彩，却忘了挑选香气；而也有些植物则恰恰相反。 还有人因为缺乏相关经验，误选了那些并不合适的花朵。他们本以为自己选的是恰当的选择，但实际上却并非如此。或许最不幸的是那些根本不知道发生了什么，整夜都在熟睡的人；他们错过了选择的机会，因此得到的花朵既没有颜色，也没有香味。 正是这样，世界上所有的花朵才拥有了它们如今所拥有的香气和颜色。 ]

rows.original: [rand|An old beggar passed through a grand city. He came to the door of a big beautiful house, with a large iron padlock on the gate. In this house lived a banker, known in the city for his miserliness; he never helped people, even though he was very rich. This very night, the miser was out upon his balcony to view the stars, and as the beggar glanced up he caught sight of the miser. "Good sir, please give me some meat or milk? No doubt the Seven will bless you for your generosity," asked the beggar. The miser replied roughly, "no, I can't! Go away!" "Maybe you can give me some wheat or beans?" kept asking the beggar, forced by hunger to humiliate himself. "I don't have anything!" said the miser. "Then give me a piece of bread, and I will be grateful," said the beggar, determined not to give up. "Go away, I don't have bread!" was the miser's reply. "At least give me some water? I'm very thirsty!" "I don't have water!" screamed the miser. "Go away, else I finally lose my patience and have you removed!" Then said the beggar, "oh, my son, why are you all the way up there? Come down to the streets and start begging food from the good people. You are even poorer than I am!" |A poor merchant dropped by a village inn to spend the night. He left aside his merchandise, and asked the innkeeper to prepare dinner. The merchant had but few wares and a couple of hawks, but the greedy innkeeper thought to herself, "why shouldn't I take all his merchandise and money?" Her covetousness continued to plague her as she prepared the merchant's meal, and finally she said to her husband, "there is a merchant staying overnight in our inn; it would would profit us to cheat him of his possessions. Surely such a poor merchant would never be able to bring down the officials on us." "There's nothing easier than that," replied her equally wicked husband. "Just put some lethe in his meal. Everyone who eats that herb forgets something, and what would a merchant forget if not his merchandise?" So that's what the greedy innkeeper did — she put the herb in the merchant's dinner, masking its bitter taste with a spicy broth. He ate the meal, thanked the innkeeper and went to bed. The merchant left the inn early the following morning. When the innkeeper woke up, she rushed to the merchant's room, but found nothing. "Oh, you fool!" she screamed at her husband. "What nonsense have you told me about this herb? The merchant forgot nothing!" "Then he must have forgotten something else!" "He forgot nothing!" "It can't be! Think about it!" The innkeeper started thinking — what could the merchant have forgotten? Suddenly she slapped herself on the forehead and said, "He forgot to pay, you old fool!" |Of No-Name Nefertiri... well, what can be said of her? Out of the slums and shanty towns of Jassira's grand capital, in the shadows of the Sultana's royal palace, a place where simple survival relied on swift hands, quick wits, and a healthy dose of stubbornness in the face of the merciless existence that wears many down to desert sand. A flash of sandy-brown fur and hair, streaked with black; two ragged, notched ears peering out from under a headwrap. It was from this place that a scruffy little catgirl emerged, rising on the backs and out of the pockets of others, armed with but a sharp dagger and an even sharper tongue. From humble beginnings of simple thievery, to fleecing the rich and miserly with dastardly cons, to waylaying the sultana's spoils of war all by her lonesome — tales that speak of a slippery catgirl who always wins, gets the girl, saves the village, steals from the corrupt and wicked, and feeds their riches to the poor. A hero to some, a scoundrel to others; No-Name Nefertiri bore the greatest bounty on her head any sultan or sultana had ever placed on a single person, and flaunted that fact with pride. There wasn't anything she couldn't steal, including the Grand Vizier's wedding ring; no vault she couldn't crack, no guard she couldn't slip past, no chase she couldn't shake. Lowlife. Blackguard. Wretch. Scumbag. No-Name Nefertiri laughed at all the epithets polite society threw at her, for they were all true to some degree. Her clothes threadbare, her boots worn, her body unadorned with anything that might give her away, the feline scoundrel never forgot where she'd come from. The people of the slums and shanties of Jassira fed her, hid her from the sultana's men, even gave their lives for her, for No-Name Nefertiri was one of their own and gave them the hope to endure one more day. And because the poor are everywhere, the tales of her exploits spread outwards from Jassira, over the sea, across the mountains, wherever there were ears willing to listen and hearts to hope. Hoping for the day where like in the tales, No-Name Nefertiri would stride into the sultana's audience chamber, before her entire court, and call her out for every wickedness she'd done in her abandonment of her divinely-appointed duties as ruler of Jassira. And though she had neither land nor lineage nor even a birth name, the self-styled Lady Nefertiri would force the sultana to recognize her title before all the nobles of Jassira. ]
rows.translation: [rand|一位老乞丐路过一座宏伟的城市。他来到一栋漂亮的大房子门前，大门上挂着一把巨大的铁锁。这栋房子里住着一位银行家，他在城里以吝啬著称——尽管他非常富有，却从不帮助别人。就在这个夜晚，这个吝啬鬼站在阳台上观赏星星，而乞丐抬头时，恰好看到了他。 尊敬的先生，请给我一些肉或牛奶吧。您的慷慨无疑会得到七神的祝福。 问那个乞丐。 那个吝啬鬼粗鲁地回答道， 不，我做不到！快走开！ 也许你可以给我一些小麦或者豆子？ 那个乞丐因为饥饿而不得不屈辱自己，不断地向别人乞讨。 我什么都没有！ 那个守财奴说道。 那就给我一块面包吧，我会很感激的。 那个乞丐说道，他决心绝不放弃。 走开，我没有面包！ 这就是那个守财奴的回答。 至少给我喝点水吧？我实在太渴了！ 我没有水了！ 那个守财奴尖叫起来。 走开，否则我真的会失去耐心，让你被赶走！ 于是，那个乞丐说道： 哦，我的儿子，你怎么会跑到那么高的地方去呢？下来到街上，向好心人讨些食物吧。你现在甚至比我还穷啊！ |一位贫穷的商人来到村里的客栈过夜。他将自己的货物放在一旁，然后让客栈老板准备晚餐。 这位商人的货物并不多，只有几件商品和几只猎鹰，但贪婪的客栈老板却在心里想 我为什么不能把他所有的商品和钱都拿走呢？ 当她为那位商人准备饭菜时，她的贪心依然困扰着她，最终她对丈夫说道： 我们客栈里住着一位商人，他打算在这里过夜。如果我们骗走他的财物，肯定会对我们有利。毕竟，这样一个穷商人根本不可能告发我们。 没有比这更简单的了。 她那同样邪恶的丈夫也这样回答了她。 只要在他的饭菜里加些莱瑟草就行了。凡是吃了这种草的人都会忘记一些事情，而一个商人如果忘记了什么，那肯定就是他经营的货物吧？ 贪婪的旅店老板就是这么做的——她把那种草药放到了商人的餐食里，用辛辣的汤汁掩盖了它的苦味。商人吃完了饭，道了谢，然后就上床睡觉了。 第二天清晨，商人早早地离开了旅店。当旅店老板醒来后，她急忙冲到商人的房间，却发现什么也没有。 哦，你这个傻瓜！ 她对丈夫大喊大叫。 你跟我说了关于这种草药的什么鬼话？那个商人可什么都没忘！ 那么他肯定还忘了别的什么！ 他什么都没忘记！ 不可能！好好想想吧！ 店主开始思考——这位商人究竟可能忘记了什么？突然，她拍了拍自己的额头，说道： 他忘了付款，你这个老傻瓜！ |关于那个无名的女子奈费尔蒂丽……嗯，又能说些什么呢？她出身于贾西拉这座大都市的贫民窟和棚户区，在苏丹娜皇家宫殿的阴影之下，那里的人们要想生存下去，就必须依靠敏捷的手指、机敏的头脑，以及在面对那无情的环境时所展现出的坚韧不拔的精神。 一抹沙棕色的毛皮，上面点缀着黑色的条纹；两只破烂不堪、带有缺口的耳朵从头巾下探了出来。就这样，一只蓬头垢面、衣衫褴褛的小猫女从这里出现了——她总是从别人的背上或口袋里钻出来，身上只带着一把锋利的匕首和一条更加锋利的舌头。 从最初简单的偷窃行为，到用卑鄙的诡计剥削富人和吝啬之徒，再到独自劫走苏丹娜的战利品——这些故事讲述的是一个狡猾的猫女如何总能取得胜利，赢得心爱的人，拯救村庄，从腐败邪恶之徒手中夺取财富，并将这些财富分发给穷人。 对某些人来说她是英雄，对另一些人而言却是无赖；无名的女法老奈费尔蒂莉所面临的通缉令，是任何苏丹或苏丹夫人曾经针对任何一个人发布的最严厉的通缉令，而她自己也以这种事实为荣。没有她偷不来的东西，包括大维齐尔的结婚戒指；没有她打不开的保险箱，没有她能够绕过的女看守，也没有任何追捕能够让她逃脱。 卑鄙小人。无赖。渣滓。混蛋。无名小卒……娜芙蒂丽对这些上流社会给她的蔑称一笑置之，因为这些称呼在某种程度上都是事实。她的衣服破旧不堪，靴子也磨破了，身上没有任何可能暴露她身份的装饰品——这个狡猾如猫的女人从未忘记自己出身何处。 贾西拉贫民窟的人们喂养她，保护她免受苏丹娜手下人的伤害，甚至有人为她献出了生命。因为无名的女法老奈费尔蒂里是他们中的一员，她给了他们继续生存下去的希望。而由于贫困无处不在，关于她的故事便从贾西拉开始传播开来，越过海洋，穿越山脉，传到了任何愿意倾听、怀有希望的地方。 人们期盼着这样一个日子：就像故事中所描述的那样，那个没有名字的奈菲尔蒂莉会走进苏丹的议事厅，在全体朝臣面前指责她抛弃了自己作为贾西拉统治者所肩负的神圣职责所犯下的种种恶行。尽管她既没有土地，也没有家族背景，甚至连一个正式的名字都没有，但这个自封为“奈菲尔蒂莉女士”的女子，一定会迫使苏丹在贾西拉的所有贵族面前承认她的地位。 ]
rows.raw: ' [rand|An old beggar passed through a grand city. He came to the door of a big beautiful house, with a large iron padlock on the gate. In this house lived a banker, known in the city for his miserliness; he never helped people, even though he was very rich. This very night, the miser was out upon his balcony to view the stars, and as the beggar glanced up he caught sight of the miser. "Good sir, please give me some meat or milk? No doubt the Seven will bless you for your generosity," asked the beggar. The miser replied roughly, "no, I can't! Go away!" "Maybe you can give me some wheat or beans?" kept asking the beggar, forced by hunger to humiliate himself. "I don't have anything!" said the miser. "Then give me a piece of bread, and I will be grateful," said the beggar, determined not to give up. "Go away, I don't have bread!" was the miser's reply. "At least give me some water? I'm very thirsty!" "I don't have water!" screamed the miser. "Go away, else I finally lose my patience and have you removed!" Then said the beggar, "oh, my son, why are you all the way up there? Come down to the streets and start begging food from the good people. You are even poorer than I am!" |A poor merchant dropped by a village inn to spend the night. He left aside his merchandise, and asked the innkeeper to prepare dinner. The merchant had but few wares and a couple of hawks, but the greedy innkeeper thought to herself, "why shouldn't I take all his merchandise and money?" Her covetousness continued to plague her as she prepared the merchant's meal, and finally she said to her husband, "there is a merchant staying overnight in our inn; it would would profit us to cheat him of his possessions. Surely such a poor merchant would never be able to bring down the officials on us." "There's nothing easier than that," replied her equally wicked husband. "Just put some lethe in his meal. Everyone who eats that herb forgets something, and what would a merchant forget if not his merchandise?" So that's what the greedy innkeeper did — she put the herb in the merchant's dinner, masking its bitter taste with a spicy broth. He ate the meal, thanked the innkeeper and went to bed. The merchant left the inn early the following morning. When the innkeeper woke up, she rushed to the merchant's room, but found nothing. "Oh, you fool!" she screamed at her husband. "What nonsense have you told me about this herb? The merchant forgot nothing!" "Then he must have forgotten something else!" "He forgot nothing!" "It can't be! Think about it!" The innkeeper started thinking — what could the merchant have forgotten? Suddenly she slapped herself on the forehead and said, "He forgot to pay, you old fool!" |Of No-Name Nefertiri... well, what can be said of her? Out of the slums and shanty towns of Jassira's grand capital, in the shadows of the Sultana's royal palace, a place where simple survival relied on swift hands, quick wits, and a healthy dose of stubbornness in the face of the merciless existence that wears many down to desert sand. A flash of sandy-brown fur and hair, streaked with black; two ragged, notched ears peering out from under a headwrap. It was from this place that a scruffy little catgirl emerged, rising on the backs and out of the pockets of others, armed with but a sharp dagger and an even sharper tongue. From humble beginnings of simple thievery, to fleecing the rich and miserly with dastardly cons, to waylaying the sultana's spoils of war all by her lonesome — tales that speak of a slippery catgirl who always wins, gets the girl, saves the village, steals from the corrupt and wicked, and feeds their riches to the poor. A hero to some, a scoundrel to others; No-Name Nefertiri bore the greatest bounty on her head any sultan or sultana had ever placed on a single person, and flaunted that fact with pride. There wasn't anything she couldn't steal, including the Grand Vizier's wedding ring; no vault she couldn't crack, no guard she couldn't slip past, no chase she couldn't shake. Lowlife. Blackguard. Wretch. Scumbag. No-Name Nefertiri laughed at all the epithets polite society threw at her, for they were all true to some degree. Her clothes threadbare, her boots worn, her body unadorned with anything that might give her away, the feline scoundrel never forgot where she'd come from. The people of the slums and shanties of Jassira fed her, hid her from the sultana's men, even gave their lives for her, for No-Name Nefertiri was one of their own and gave them the hope to endure one more day. And because the poor are everywhere, the tales of her exploits spread outwards from Jassira, over the sea, across the mountains, wherever there were ears willing to listen and hearts to hope. Hoping for the day where like in the tales, No-Name Nefertiri would stride into the sultana's audience chamber, before her entire court, and call her out for every wickedness she'd done in her abandonment of her divinely-appointed duties as ruler of Jassira. And though she had neither land nor lineage nor even a birth name, the self-styled Lady Nefertiri would force the sultana to recognize her title before all the nobles of Jassira. ]'

rows.original: As Kiyoko continues cradling your [var0|son|daughter], the little fox kit wiggles in her grasp and snuffles at her breast, giving the milk-filled mounds a nip and nuzzle. Instinctively, the kitsune raises the little one to her nipple, and sighs happily as the fox kit latches on and begins to nurse. After a few moments, it readily becomes apparent that there's more going on here than the simple nursing of a newborn. Before your eyes, the newborn fox kit begins to grow rapidly, personality and nutrition alike flowing from Kiyoko's breast into your [var0|son|daughter]. In the blink of an eye, Kiyoko is no longer cradling her newest child, but instead is supporting [var0|him|her] on her lap as both of her breasts are drained in quick, hungry succession. At the same time, her leftover pregnant belly slowly shrinks back into nothingness, contracting in steady pulses until Kiyoko's midriff is flat and trim once more. When it's all over and your [var0|son|daughter] pops free, [var0|he|she] looks to be a young child of about six to seven years old — not quite the dramatic growth to maturity that some Wraith-touched races of beastkin go through, but enough for Kiyoko to shake her head in wonder at the whole scene. "I swear, no matter how long I live here, I'll never understand how the Astral Plane works, how it changes even the most mundane of things." You look at the two-tailed kitsune child that your [var0|son|daughter] now is, then back at Kiyoko, who gives you a small smile and shrug before unsteadily easing your [var0|son|daughter] off her lap and pushing herself to her feet. Should she be standing so soon after the birth? "I-I'll be fine. Although I'm sorry, [pc.name]. While I do look forward to your visits, I do think that I won't be feeling up to very much today, for obvious reasons." Her eyes wander down to your child by her side, and the little two-tailed kitsune [var0|boy|girl] gives you an uncertain smile in return, apparently completely unconcerned with being utterly naked save for a towel. You see. "I've got to get our [var0|son|daughter] settled in, then look to taking a long, long nap, followed by some hot broth. [pc.name], could you please see yourself out? Again, I apologize if it looks like I'm shooing you away -" Oh no, that won't be any problem at all. The Astral Plane will provide her with everything she needs, you take it? "Yes. Once again, [pc.name], thank you for doing this for me. For us." She looks down at her new [var0|son|daughter]. "Perhaps we'll play some during your next visit."
rows.translation: 当清子继续怀抱着你 [var0|儿子|女儿]小狐妖在她的怀里扭动身体，用鼻子蹭她的胸部，轻轻啃咬那些充满乳汁的乳头。出于本能，那只小狐妖将头凑到她的乳头上，当它开始吮吸乳汁时，她幸福地叹了口气。 过了一会儿，你很快就会发现，这里发生的事情远不止是简单的哺乳那么简单。在你眼前，这只新生的小狐妖开始迅速成长，它的性格和营养都来自于清子的乳房 [var0|儿子|女儿]转眼间，清子已经不再抱着她的新宝宝，而是开始搀扶着它了。 [var0|他|她] 当这一切结束时，你的 [var0|儿子|女儿] 弹了出来。 [var0|他|她] 看起来应该是一个六七岁左右的幼童——虽然不像某些被“怨灵”影响的兽人种族那样会经历如此剧烈的成长过程，但这样的变化也已经足以让清子对这一幕感到惊叹不已了。 我发誓，无论我在这里生活多久，我也永远无法理解星界是如何运作的，它是如何改变那些最平凡的事物 的。 你看着那个有着双尾的狐妖小孩 [var0|儿子|女儿] 现在回到清子身上，她微微一笑，耸了耸肩，然后有些不稳地松开了你的手 [var0|儿子|女儿] 从她的腿上爬下来，然后站了起来。 分娩后这么快就让她站立，这样合适吗？ 我、我不会有事的。虽然很抱歉， [pc.name]虽然我确实很期待你们的到访，但出于一些显而易见的原因，我想今天我应该不太能招待你们了。 她的目光落在你身旁的孩子身上，还有那只小小的双尾狐 [var0|男孩|女孩] 她回以一个不确定的微笑，显然完全不在意自己除了浴巾之外一丝不挂的事实。 你懂的吧。 我得去把我们的……拿过来。 [var0|儿子|女儿] 安顿下来后，就可以美美地小睡一会儿，然后再喝一些热汤。 [pc.name]请您自己出去吧。再次为我的言行可能让您觉得我在赶您走而道歉…… 哦不，那根本不是什么问题。星界将会为她提供所需的一切，你明白我的意思吧？ 是的。再一次， [pc.name]谢谢你为我，也为我们做了这一切。 她低头看了看自己的新物品。 [var0|儿子|女儿]. 也许在你下次来的时候，我们可以一起玩一些游戏。
